entries.b1a0e3916d68a169163cad0e73047d746a661bd0: <div sID="gen21863" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Matt.9" sID="Matt.9"/> <div eID="gen21863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21864" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21865" type="x-p"/> We have in this chapter remarkable instances of the power and pity of the Lord Jesus, sufficient to convince us that he is both able to save to the uttermost all that come to God by him, and as willing as he is able. His power and pity appear here in the good offices he did, I. To the bodies of people, in curing the palsy (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.2-Matt.9.8">ver. 2-8</reference>); raising to life the ruler's daughter, and healing the bloody issue (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.18-Matt.9.26">ver. 18-26</reference>); giving sight to two blind men (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.27-Matt.9.31">ver. 27-31</reference>); casting the devil out of one possessed (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.32-Matt.9.34">ver. 32-34</reference>); and healing all manner of sickness, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.35">ver. 35</reference>. II. To the souls of people; in forgiving sins (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">ver. 2</reference>); calling Matthew, and conversing freely with publicans and sinners (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.9-Matt.9.13">ver. 9-13</reference>); considering the frame of his disciples, with reference to the duty of fasting (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.14-Matt.9.17">ver. 14-17</reference>); preaching the gospel, and, in compassion to the multitude, providing preachers for them, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.35-Matt.9.38">ver. 35-38</reference>. Thus did he prove himself to be, as undoubtedly he is, the skilful, faithful Physician, both of soul and body, who has sufficient remedies for all the maladies of both: for which we must, therefore, apply ourselves to him, and glorify him both with our bodies and with our spirits, which are his, in return to him for his kindness to both.
entries.22a91f92a74e63544d068c4195921470d55e98e7: <div eID="gen21865" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21864" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Heals a Man Sick of the Palsy.</title> <div sID="gen21866" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And he entered into a ship, and passed over, and came into his own city. <hi type="super">2</hi> And, behold, they brought to him a man sick of the palsy, lying on a bed: and Jesus seeing their faith said unto the sick of the palsy; Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee. <hi type="super">3</hi> And, behold, certain of the scribes said within themselves, This <hi type="italic">man</hi> blasphemeth. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Jesus knowing their thoughts said, Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts? <hi type="super">5</hi> For whether is easier, to say, <hi type="italic">Thy</hi> sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and walk? <hi type="super">6</hi> But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he arose, and departed to his house. 8 But when the multitudes saw <hi type="italic">it,</hi> they marvelled, and glorified God, which had given such power unto men. <div eID="gen21866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21867" type="x-p"/> The first words of this chapter oblige us to look back to the close of that which precedes it, where we find the Gadarenes so resenting the loss of their swine, that they were disgusted with Christ's company, and besought him to <hi type="italic">depart out of their coasts.</hi> Now here it follows, <hi type="italic">He entered into a ship, and passed over.</hi> They bid him begone, and he took them at their word, and we never read that he came into their coasts again. Now here observe, 1. His justice—that he left them. Note, Christ will not tarry long where he is not welcome. In righteous judgment, he forsakes those places and persons that are weary of him, but abides with those that covet and court his stay. <hi type="italic">If the unbeliever will depart</hi> from Christ, <hi type="italic">let him depart;</hi> it is at his peril, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.15">1 Cor. vii. 15</reference>. 2. His patience—that he did not leave some destroying judgment behind him, to punish them, as they deserved, for their contempt and contumacy. How easily, how justly, might he have sent them after their swine, who were already so much under the devil's power. The provocation, indeed, was very great: but he put it up, and passed it by; and, without any angry resentments or upbraidings, he <hi type="italic">entered into a ship, and passed over.</hi> This was the day of his patience; he came not to <hi type="italic">destroy men's lives,</hi> but to save them; not to kill, but to cure. Spiritual judgments agree more with the constitution of gospel times; yet some observe, that in those bloody wars which the Romans made upon the Jews, which began not many years after this, they first besieged the town of Gadara, where these Gadarenes dwelt. Note, Those that drive Christ from them, draw all miseries upon them. Woe unto us, if God depart from us. <div eID="gen21867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21868" type="x-p"/> He came <hi type="italic">into his own city, Capernaum,</hi> the principal place of his residence at present (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.1">Mark ii. 1</reference>), and therefore called <hi type="italic">his own city.</hi> He had himself testified, that a prophet it least honoured in <hi type="italic">his own country</hi> and <hi type="italic">city,</hi> yet thither he came; for he <hi type="italic">sought not his own honour;</hi> but, being in a state of humiliation, he was content to be despised of the people. At Capernaum all the circumstances recorded in this chapter happened, and are, therefore, put together here, though, in the harmony of the evangelists, other events intervened. When the Gadarenes desired Christ to depart, they of Capernaum received him. If Christ be affronted by some, there are others in whom he will be glorious; if one will not, another will. <div eID="gen21868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21869" type="x-p"/> Now the first occurrence, after Christ's return to Capernaum, as recorded in <reference osisRef="Matt.9.1-Matt.9.8">these verses</reference>, was the cure of the man sick of the palsy. In which we may observe, <div eID="gen21869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21870" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">faith of his friends</hi> in bringing him to Christ. His distemper was such, that he could not come to Christ himself, but as he was carried. Note, Even the halt and the lame may be brought to Christ, and they shall not be rejected by him. If we do as well as we can, he will accept of us. Christ had an eye to their faith. Little children cannot go to Christ themselves, but he will have an eye to the faith of those that bring them, and it shall not be in vain. <hi type="italic">Jesus saw their faith,</hi> the faith of the paralytic himself, as well as of them that brought him; Jesus saw the habit of faith, though his distemper, perhaps, impaired his intellect, and obstructed the actings of it. Now their faith was, 1. A strong faith; they firmly believed that Jesus Christ both could and would heal him; else they would not have brought the sick man to him so publicly, and through so much difficulty. 2. A humble faith; though the sick man was unable to stir a step, they would not ask Christ to make him a visit, but brought him to attend on Christ. It is fitter than we should wait on Christ, than he on us. 3. An active faith: in the belief of Christ's power and goodness, they brought the sick man to him, <hi type="italic">lying on a bed,</hi> which could not be done without a deal of pains. Note, A strong faith regards no obstacles in pressing after Christ. <div eID="gen21870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21871" type="x-p"/> II. The <hi type="italic">favour of Christ,</hi> in what he said to him; <hi type="italic">Son, be of good cheer, thy sins be forgiven thee.</hi> This was a sovereign cordial to a sick man, and was enough to <hi type="italic">make all his bed in his sickness;</hi> and to make it easy to him. We read not of any thing said to Christ; probably the poor sick man could not speak for himself, and they that brought him chose rather to speak by actions than words; they set him before Christ; that was enough. Note, It is not in vain to present ourselves and our friends to Christ, as the objects of his pity. Misery cries as well as sin, and mercy is no less quick of hearing than justice. Here is, in what Christ said, 1. A kind compellation; <hi type="italic">Son.</hi> Note, Exhortations and consolations to the afflicted speak to them as to sons, for afflictions are fatherly discipline, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.5">Heb. xii. 5</reference>. 2. A gracious encouragement; "<hi type="italic">Be of good cheer. Have a good heart on it;</hi> cheer up thy spirits." Probably the poor man, when let down among them all in his bed, was put out of countenance, was afraid of a rebuke for being brought in so rudely: but Christ does not stand upon ceremony; he bids him <hi type="italic">be of good cheer;</hi> all would be well, he should not be laid before Christ in vain. Christ bids him <hi type="italic">be of good cheer;</hi> and then cures him. He would have those to whom he deals his gifts, to be cheerful in seeking him, and in trusting in him; to be of good courage. 3. A good reason for that encouragement; <hi type="italic">Thy sins are forgiven thee.</hi> Now this may be considered, (1.) as an introduction to the cure of his bodily distemper; "Thy sins are <hi type="italic">pardoned,</hi> and therefore thou shalt be healed." Note, As sin is the cause of sickness, so the remission of sin is the comfort of recovery from sickness; not but that sin may be pardoned, and yet the sickness not removed; not but that the sickness may be removed, and yet the sin not pardoned: but if we have the comfort of our reconciliation to God, with the comfort of our recovery from sickness, this makes it a mercy indeed to us, as to Hezekiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.17">Isa. xxxviii. 17</reference>. Or, (2.) As a reason of the command to <hi type="italic">be of good cheer,</hi> whether he were cured of his disease or not; "Though I should not heal thee, wilt thou not say thou hast not sought in vain, if I assure thee that <hi type="italic">thy sins are pardoned;</hi> and wilt thou not look upon that as a sufficient ground of comfort, though thou shouldst continue <hi type="italic">sick of the palsy?</hi>" Note, They who, through grace, have some evidence of the forgiveness of their sins, have reasons to be of good cheer, whatever outward troubles or afflictions they are under; see <reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Isa. xxxiii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen21871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21872" type="x-p"/> III. The <hi type="italic">cavil of the scribes</hi> at that which Christ said (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.3">v. 3</reference>); They <hi type="italic">said within themselves,</hi> in their hearts, <hi type="italic">among themselves,</hi> in their secret whisperings, <hi type="italic">This man blasphemeth.</hi> See how the greatest instance of heaven's power and grace is branded with the blackest note of hell's enmity; Christ's pardoning sin is termed blasphemy; nor had it been less, if he had not had commission from God for it. They, therefore, are guilty of blasphemy, that have no such commission, and yet pretend to pardon sin. <div eID="gen21872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21873" type="x-p"/> IV. The conviction which Christ gave them of the unreasonableness of this cavil, before he proceeded. <div eID="gen21873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21874" type="x-p"/> 1. He <hi type="italic">charged them with it.</hi> Though they did but say it within themselves, he <hi type="italic">knew their thoughts.</hi> Note, Our Lord Jesus has the perfect knowledge of all that we say within ourselves. Thoughts are secret and sudden, yet naked and open before Christ, the eternal Word (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.12-Heb.4.13">Heb. iv. 12, 13</reference>), and he <hi type="italic">understands them afar off,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.139.2">Ps. cxxxix. 2</reference>. He could say to them (which no mere man could), <hi type="italic">Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?</hi> Note, There is a great deal of evil in sinful thoughts, which is very offensive to the Lord Jesus. He being the Sovereign of the heart, sinful thoughts invade his right, and disturb his possession; therefore he takes notice of them, and is much displeased with them. In them lies the <hi type="italic">root of bitterness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.5">Gen. vi. 5</reference>. The sins that begin and end in the heart, and go no further, are as dangerous as any other. <div eID="gen21874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21875" type="x-p"/> 2. He <hi type="italic">argued them out of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.9.5-Matt.9.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Where observe, <div eID="gen21875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21876" type="x-p"/> (1.) How he <hi type="italic">asserts</hi> his authority in the <hi type="italic">kingdom of grace.</hi> He undertakes to make out, that the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> the Mediator, has <hi type="italic">power on earth to forgive sins;</hi> for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> the Father has <hi type="italic">committed all judgment to the Son,</hi> and has given him this authority, <hi type="italic">because he is the Son of man,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.22">John v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>. If he has <hi type="italic">power to give eternal life,</hi> as he certainly has (<reference osisRef="John.17.2">John xvii. 2</reference>), he must have power to forgive sin; for guilt is a bar that must be removed, or we can never get to heaven. What an encouragement is this to poor sinners to repent, that the power of pardoning sin is put into the hands of the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> who is bone of our bone! And if he had this <hi type="italic">power on earth,</hi> much more now that he is exalted to the Father's right hand, to give <hi type="italic">repentance and remission of sins,</hi> and so to be both <hi type="italic">a Prince and a Saviour,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.5.31">Acts v. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen21876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21877" type="x-p"/> (2.) How he <hi type="italic">proves</hi> it, by his power in the kingdom of nature; his power to cure diseases. Is it not as easy to say, <hi type="italic">Thy sins are forgiven thee,</hi> as to say, <hi type="italic">Arise and walk?</hi> He that can cure the disease, whether <hi type="italic">declaratively</hi> as a Prophet, or <hi type="italic">authoritatively</hi> as God, can, in like manner, forgive the sin. Now, [1.] This is a general argument to prove that Christ had a divine mission. His miracles, especially his miraculous cures, confirm what he said of himself, that he was the Son of God; the <hi type="italic">power</hi> that appeared in his cures proved him <hi type="italic">sent of God;</hi> and the <hi type="italic">pity</hi> that appeared in them proved him sent of God <hi type="italic">to heal and save.</hi> The God of truth would not set his seal to a lie. [2.] It had a particular cogency in this case. The palsy was but a symptom of the disease of sin; now he made it to appear, that he could effectually cure the original disease, by the immediate removal of that symptom; so close a connection was there between the sin and the sickness. He that had power to remove the punishment, no doubt, had power to remit the sin. The scribes stood much upon a legal righteousness, and placed their confidence in that, and made no great matter of the <hi type="italic">forgiveness of sin,</hi> the doctrine upon which Christ hereby designed to put honour, and to show that his great errand to the world was to <hi type="italic">save his people from their sins.</hi> <div eID="gen21877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21878" type="x-p"/> V. The immediate cure of the sick man. Christ turned from disputing with them, and spake healing to him. The most necessary arguings must not divert us from doing the good that our <hi type="italic">hand finds to do.</hi> He saith to <hi type="italic">the sick of the palsy, Arise, take up thy bed, and go to thine house;</hi> and a healing, quickening, strengthening power accompanied this word (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">he arose and departed to his house.</hi> Now, 1. Christ bid him <hi type="italic">take up his bed,</hi> to show that he was <hi type="italic">perfectly cured,</hi> and that not only he had no more occasion to be <hi type="italic">carried</hi> upon his bed, but that he had strength to <hi type="italic">carry it.</hi> 2. He sent him to <hi type="italic">his house,</hi> to be a blessing to his family, where he had been so long a burden; and did not take him along with him for a show, which those would do in such a case who seek the honour that comes from men. <div eID="gen21878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21879" type="x-p"/> VI. The impression which this made upon the multitude (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.8">v. 8</reference>); they <hi type="italic">marvelled,</hi> and <hi type="italic">glorified God.</hi> Note, All our wonder should help to enlarge our hearts in <hi type="italic">glorifying God,</hi> who alone does marvellous things. They glorified God for what he had done for this poor man. Note, Others' mercies should be our praises, and we should give him thanks for them, for we are members one of another. Though few of this multitude were so convinced, as to be brought to believe in Christ, and to follow him, yet they admired him, not as God, or the Son of God, but as a <hi type="italic">man</hi> to whom God <hi type="italic">had given such power.</hi> Note, God must be glorified in all the power that is <hi type="italic">given to men</hi> to do good. For all power is originally his; it is in him, as the Fountain, in men, as the cisterns.
entries.c09f74e5b9c59441bb68800108ddb039531b76ff: <div eID="gen21879" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Matthew Called.</title> <div sID="gen21880" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him. <hi type="super">10</hi> And it came to pass, as Jesus sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples. <hi type="super">11</hi> And when the Pharisees saw <hi type="italic">it,</hi> they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners? <hi type="super">12</hi> But when Jesus heard <hi type="italic">that,</hi> he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick. <hi type="super">13</hi> But go ye and learn what <hi type="italic">that</hi> meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. <div eID="gen21880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21881" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have an account of the grace and favour of Christ to poor publicans, particularly to Matthew. What he did to the bodies of people was to make way for a kind design upon their souls. Now observe here, <div eID="gen21881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21882" type="x-p"/> I. The call of Matthew, the penman of this gospel. Mark and Luke call him Levi; it was ordinary for the same person to have two names: perhaps Matthew was the name he was most known by as a publican, and, therefore, in his humility, he called himself by that name, rather than by the more honourable name of Levi. Some think Christ gave him the name of Matthew when he called him to be an apostle; as Simon, he surnamed Peter. Matthew signifies, <hi type="italic">the gift of God,</hi> Ministers are God's gifts to the church; their ministry, and their ability for it, are God's gifts to them. Now observe, <div eID="gen21882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21883" type="x-p"/> 1. The posture that Christ's call found Matthew in. He was <hi type="italic">sitting at the receipt of custom,</hi> for he was a publican, <reference osisRef="Luke.5.27">Luke v. 27</reference>. He was a custom-house officer at the port of Capernaum, or an exciseman, or collector of the land-tax. Now, (1.) He was in his calling, as the rest of them whom Christ called, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.18">ch. iv. 18</reference>. Note, As Satan chooses to come, with his temptations, to those that are idle, so Christ chooses to come, with his calls, to those that are employed. But, (2.) It was a calling of ill fame among serious people; because it was attended with so much corruption and temptation, and there were so few in that business that were honest men. Matthew himself owns what he was before his conversion, as does St. Paul (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13">1 Tim. i. 13</reference>), that the grace of Christ in calling him might be the more magnified, and to show, that God has his remnant among all sorts of people. None can justify themselves in their unbelief, by their calling in the world; for there is no <hi type="italic">sinful</hi> calling, but some have been saved <hi type="italic">out of it,</hi> and no <hi type="italic">lawful calling,</hi> but some have been saved <hi type="italic">in it.</hi> <div eID="gen21883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21884" type="x-p"/> 2. The preventing power of this call. We find not that Matthew looked after Christ, or had any inclination to follow him, though some of his kindred were already disciples of Christ, but Christ prevented him with the blessings of his goodness. He is found of those that seek him not. Christ <hi type="italic">spoke first;</hi> we have not chosen him, but he hath chosen us. He said, <hi type="italic">Follow me;</hi> and the same divine, almighty power accompanied this word to convert Matthew, which attended that word (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Arise and walk,</hi> to cure the man sick of the palsy. Note, A saving change is wrought in the soul by Christ as the <hi type="italic">Author,</hi> and his word as the <hi type="italic">means.</hi> His gospel is the <hi type="italic">power of God unto salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Rom. i. 16</reference>. The call was effectual, for he came at the call; <hi type="italic">he arose, and</hi> followed him immediately; neither denied, nor deferred his obedience. The power of divine grace soon answers and overcomes all objections. Neither his commission for his place, nor his gains by it, could detain him, when Christ called him. <hi type="italic">He conferred not with flesh and blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.1.15-Gal.1.16">Gal. i. 15, 16</reference>. He quitted his post, and his hopes of preferment in that way; and, though we find the disciples that were fishers occasionally fishing again afterwards, we never find Matthew at the receipt of custom again. <div eID="gen21884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21885" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's converse with publicans and sinners upon this occasion; Christ called Matthew, to introduce himself into an acquaintance with the people of that profession. <hi type="italic">Jesus sat at meat in the house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.9.10">v. 10</reference>. The other evangelists tell us, that Matthew made a <hi type="italic">great feast,</hi> which the poor fishermen, when they were called, were not able to do. But when he comes to speak of this himself, he neither tells us that it was his own house, nor that it was a feast, but only that he <hi type="italic">sat at meat in the house;</hi> preserving the remembrance of Christ's favours to the publicans, rather than of the respect he had paid to Christ. Note, It well becomes us to speak sparingly of our own good deeds. <div eID="gen21885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21886" type="x-p"/> Now observe, 1. When Matthew invited Christ, he invited his disciples to <hi type="italic">come along with him.</hi> Note, They that welcome Christ, must welcome all that are his, for his sake, and let them have a room in their hearts. 2. He invited many publicans and sinners to <hi type="italic">meet him.</hi> This was the chief thing Matthew aimed at in this treat, that he might have an opportunity of bringing his old associates acquainted with Christ. He knew by experience what the grace of Christ could do, and would not despair concerning them. Note, They who are effectually brought to Christ themselves, cannot but be desirous that others also may be brought to him, and ambitious of contributing something towards it. True grace will not contentedly eat its morsels alone, but will invite others. When by the conversion of Matthew the fraternity was broken, presently his house was filled with publicans, and surely some of them will <hi type="italic">follow him,</hi> as he <hi type="italic">followed Christ.</hi> Thus did Andrew and Philip, <reference osisRef="John.1.41 John.1.45">John i. 41, 45</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.29">iv. 29</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Judg.14.9">Judges xiv. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen21886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21887" type="x-p"/> III. The displeasure of the Pharisees at this, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.11">v. 11</reference>. They cavilled at it; <hi type="italic">why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?</hi> Here observe, 1. That Christ was quarrelled with. It was not the least of his sufferings, that he <hi type="italic">endured the contradiction of sinners against himself.</hi> None was more quarrelled with by men, than he that came to take up the great quarrel between God and man. Thus he denied himself the honour due to an incarnate Deity, which was to be justified in what he spake, and to have all he said readily subscribed to: for though he never spoke or did anything amiss, every thing he said and did was found fault with. Thus he taught us to expect and prepare for reproach, and to bear it patiently. 2. They that quarrelled with him were the Pharisees; a proud generation of men, conceited of themselves, and censorious of others; of the same temper with those in the prophet's time, who said, <hi type="italic">Stand by thyself, come not near me; I am holier than thou:</hi> they were very strict in avoiding <hi type="italic">sinners,</hi> but not in avoiding <hi type="italic">sin;</hi> none greater zealots than they for the <hi type="italic">form</hi> of godliness, nor greater enemies to the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of it. They were for keeping up the traditions of the elders to a nicety, and so propagating the same spirit that they were themselves governed by. 3. They brought their cavil, not to Christ himself; they had not the courage to face him with it, but to his disciples. The disciples were in the same company, but the quarrel is with the Master: for they would not have done it, if he had not; and they thought it worse in him who was a prophet, than in them; his dignity, they thought, should set him at a greater distance from such company than others. Being offended at the Master, they quarrel with the disciples. Note, It concerns Christians to be able to vindicate and justify Christ, and his doctrines and laws, and to be <hi type="italic">ready always to give an answer to those that ask them a reason of the hope that is in them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1 Pet. iii. 15</reference>. While he is an Advocate for us in heaven, let us be advocates for him on earth, and make his reproach our own. 4. The complaint was his <hi type="italic">eating with publicans and sinners:</hi> to be intimate with wicked people is against the law of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.115">Ps. cxix. 115</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">i. 1</reference>); and perhaps by accusing Christ of this to his disciples, they hoped to tempt them from him, to put them out of conceit with him, and so to bring them over to themselves to be their disciples, who kept better company; for they <hi type="italic">compassed sea and land to make proselytes.</hi> To be intimate with publicans was against the <hi type="italic">tradition of the elders,</hi> and, therefore, they looked upon it as a heinous thing. They were angry with Christ for this, (1.) Because they <hi type="italic">wished ill to him,</hi> and sought occasion to misrepresent him. Note, It is an easy and very common thing to put the worst constructions upon the best words and actions. (2.) Because they <hi type="italic">wished no good to</hi> publicans and sinners, but envied Christ's favour to them, and were grieved to see them brought to repentance. Note, It may justly be suspected, that they have not the grace of God themselves, who grudge others a share in that grace, who are not pleased with it. <div eID="gen21887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21888" type="x-p"/> IV. The defence that Christ made for himself and his disciples, in justification of their converse with publicans and sinners. The disciples, it should seem, being yet weak, had to seek for an answer to the Pharisees' cavil, and, therefore, bring it to Christ, and he heard it (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.12">v. 12</reference>), or perhaps overheard them whispering it to his disciples. Let him alone to vindicate himself and to plead his own cause, to answer for himself and for us too. Two things he urges in his defence, <div eID="gen21888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21889" type="x-p"/> 1. The necessity and exigence of the case of the publicans, which called aloud for his help, and therefore justified him in conversing with them for their good. It was the extreme necessity of poor, lost sinners, that brought Christ from the pure regions above, to these impure ones; and the same was it, that brought him into this company which was thought impure. Now, <div eID="gen21889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21890" type="x-p"/> (1.) He proves the necessity of the case of the publicans: <hi type="italic">they that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.</hi> The publicans are sick, and they need one to help and heal them, which the Pharisees think they do not. Note, <div eID="gen21890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21891" type="x-p"/> [1.] Sin is the sickness of the soul; sinners are spiritually sick. Original corruptions are the diseases of the soul, actual transgressions are its wounds, or the eruptions of the disease. It is deforming, weakening, disquieting, wasting, killing, but, blessed be God, not incurable. [2.] Jesus Christ is the great Physician of souls. His curing of bodily diseases signified this, that he arose with <hi type="italic">healing under his wings.</hi> He is a skilful, faithful, compassionate Physician, and it is his office and business to heal the sick. Wise and good men should be as physicians to all about them; Christ was so. <hi type="italic">Hunc affectum versus omnes habet sapiens, quem versus ægros suos medicus—A wise man cherishes towards all around him the feelings of a physician for his patient.</hi> Seneca <hi type="italic">De Const.</hi> [3.] Sin-sick souls have need of this Physician, for their disease is dangerous; nature will not help itself; no man can help us; such need have we of Christ, that we are undone, eternally undone, without him. Sensible sinners see their need, and apply themselves to him accordingly. [4.] There are multitudes who fancy themselves to be sound and whole, who think they have <hi type="italic">no need of Christ,</hi> but that they can shift for themselves well enough without him, as Laodicea, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.17">Rev. iii. 17</reference>. Thus the Pharisees desired not the knowledge of Christ's word and ways, not because they had no need of him, but because they thought they had none. See <reference osisRef="John.9.40-John.9.41">John ix. 40, 41</reference>. <div eID="gen21891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21892" type="x-p"/> (2.) He proves, that their necessity did sufficiently justify his conduct, in conversing familiarly with them, and that he ought not to be blamed for it; for that necessity made it <hi type="italic">an act of charity,</hi> which ought always to be preferred before the formalities of a religious profession, in which <hi type="italic">bene</hi>ficence and <hi type="italic">muni</hi>ficence are far better than <hi type="italic">magni</hi>ficence, as much as substance is better than shows or shadows. Those duties, which are of moral and natural obligation, are to take place even of those divine laws which are positive and ritual, much more of those impositions of men, and traditions of the elders, which make God's law stricter than he has made it. This he proves (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">v. 13</reference>) by a passage quoted out of <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Hos. vi. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will have mercy and not sacrifice.</hi> That morose separation from the society of publicans, which the Pharisees enjoined, was <hi type="italic">less than sacrifice;</hi> but Christ's conversing with them was more than an act of common mercy, and therefore to be preferred before it. If to do well ourselves is better than sacrifice, as Samuel shows (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22-1Sam.15.23">1 Sam. xv. 22, 23</reference>), much more to do good to others. Christ's conversing with sinners is here called mercy: to promote the conversion of souls is the greatest act of mercy imaginable; it is <hi type="italic">saving a soul from death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.20">Jam. v. 20</reference>. Observe how Christ quotes this, <hi type="italic">Go ye and learn what that meaneth.</hi> Note, It is not enough to be acquainted with the letter of scripture, but we must learn to understand the meaning of it. And they have best learned the meaning of the scriptures, that have learned how to apply them as a reproof to their own faults, and a rule for their own practice. This scripture which Christ quoted, served not only to vindicate him, but, [1.] To show wherein true religion consists; not in external observances: not <hi type="italic">in meats and drinks</hi> and shows of sanctity, not in little particular opinions and doubtful disputations, but in doing all the good we can to the bodies and souls of others; in righteousness and peace; in <hi type="italic">visiting the fatherless and widows.</hi> [2.] To condemn the Pharisaical hypocrisy of those who place religion in rituals, more than in morals, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.23">ch. xxiii. 23</reference>. They espouse those forms of godliness which may be made consistent with, and perhaps subservient to, their pride, covetousness, ambition, and malice, while they hate that power of it which is mortifying to those lusts. <div eID="gen21892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21893" type="x-p"/> 2. He urges the nature and end of his own commission. He must keep to his orders, and prosecute that for which he was appointed to be the great Teacher; now, says he, "<hi type="italic">I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance,</hi> and therefore must converse with publicans." Observe, (1.) What his errand was; it was to <hi type="italic">call to repentance.</hi> This was his first text (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.17">ch. iv. 17</reference>), and it was the tendency of all his sermons. Note, The gospel call is a call to repentance; a call to us to change our mind and to change our way. (2.) With whom his errand lay; not with <hi type="italic">the righteous,</hi> but with <hi type="italic">sinners.</hi> That is, [1.] If the children of men had not been <hi type="italic">sinners,</hi> there had been no occasion for Christ's coming among them. He is the Saviour, not of man as <hi type="italic">man,</hi> but of man as <hi type="italic">fallen.</hi> Had the first Adam continued in his original <hi type="italic">righteousness,</hi> we had not needed a second Adam. [2.] Therefore his <hi type="italic">greatest business</hi> lies with the <hi type="italic">greatest sinners;</hi> the more dangerous the sick man's case is, the more occasion there is for the physician's help. Christ came into the world to <hi type="italic">save sinners,</hi> but especially <hi type="italic">the chief</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1 Tim. i. 15</reference>); to call not those so much, who, though sinners, are comparatively righteous, but the worst of sinners. [3.] The more sensible any sinners are of their sinfulness, the more welcome will Christ and his gospel be to them; and every one chooses to go where his company is desired, not to those who would rather have his room. Christ came not with an expectation of succeeding among <hi type="italic">the righteous,</hi> those who conceit themselves so, and therefore will sooner be sick of their Saviour, than sick of their sins, but among the convinced humble <hi type="italic">sinners;</hi> to them Christ will come, for to them he will be welcome.
entries.981a3037ca5b5b83969eb1f7d749a4e9a8b6216a: <div eID="gen21893" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Reply to the Disciples of John.</title> <div sID="gen21894" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Then came to him the disciples of John, saying, Why do we and the Pharisees fast oft, but thy disciples fast not? <hi type="super">15</hi> And Jesus said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast. <hi type="super">16</hi> No man putteth a piece of new cloth unto an old garment, for that which is put in to fill it up taketh from the garment, and the rent is made worse. <hi type="super">17</hi> Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved. <div eID="gen21894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21895" type="x-p"/> The objections which were made against Christ and his disciples gave occasion to some of the most profitable of his discourses; thus are the interests of truth often served, even by the opposition it meets with from gainsayers, and thus the wisdom of Christ brings good out of evil. This is the third instance of it in this chapter; his discourse of his power to forgive sin, and his readiness to receive sinners, was occasioned by the cavils of the scribes and Pharisees; so here, from a reflection upon the conduct of his family, arose a discourse concerning his tenderness for it. Observe, <div eID="gen21895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21896" type="x-p"/> I. The objection which the disciples of John made against Christ's disciples, for not fasting so often as they did; which they are charged with, as another instance of the looseness of their profession, besides that of eating with publicans and sinners; and it is therefore suggested to them, that they should change that profession for another more strict. It appears by the other evangelists (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.18">Mark ii. 18</reference> and <reference osisRef="Luke.5.33">Luke v. 33</reference>) that the disciples of the Pharisees joined with them, and we have reason to suspect that they instigated them, making use of John's disciples as their spokesmen, because they, being more in favour with Christ and his disciples, could do it more plausibly. Note, It is no new thing for bad men to set good men together by the ears; if the people of God differ in their sentiments, designing men will take that occasion to sow discord, and to incense them one against another, and alienate them one from another, and so make an easy prey of them. If the disciples of John and of Jesus clash, we have reason to suspect the Pharisees have been at work underhand, blowing the coals. Now the complaint is, <hi type="italic">Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but thy disciples fast not?</hi> It is pity the duties of religion, which ought to be the confirmations of holy love, should be made the occasions of strife and contention; but they often are so, as here; where we may observe, <div eID="gen21896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21897" type="x-p"/> 1. How they boasted of their own fasting. <hi type="italic">We and the Pharisees fast often.</hi> Fasting has in all ages of the church been consecrated, upon special occasions, to the service of religion; the Pharisees were much in it; many of them kept two fast-days in a week, and yet the generality of them were hypocrites and bad men. Note, False and formal professors often excel others in outward acts of devotion, and even of mortification. The disciples of John <hi type="italic">fasted often,</hi> partly in compliance with their master's practice, for he came <hi type="italic">neither eating nor drinking</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.18">ch. xi. 18</reference>); and people are apt to imitate their leaders, though not always from the same inward principle; partly in compliance with their master's doctrine of repentance. Note, The severer part of religion is often most <hi type="italic">minded</hi> by those that are yet under the discipline of the Spirit, as a <hi type="italic">Spirit of bondage,</hi> whereas, though these are good in their place, we must pass through them to that life of delight in God and dependence on him, to which these should lead. Now they come to Christ to tell him that they <hi type="italic">fasted often,</hi> at least they thought it often. Note, <hi type="italic">Most men will proclaim every one his own goodness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.6">Prov. xx. 6</reference>. There is a proneness in professors to brag of their own performance in religion, especially if there by any thing extraordinary in them; nay, and not only to boast of them before men, but to plead them before God, and confide in them as a righteousness. <div eID="gen21897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21898" type="x-p"/> 2. How they blamed Christ's disciples for not fasting so often as they did. <hi type="italic">Thy disciples fast not.</hi> They could not but know, that Christ had instructed his disciples to keep their fasts private, and to manage themselves so as that they might not <hi type="italic">appear unto men to fast;</hi> and, therefore, it was very uncharitable in them to conclude they did <hi type="italic">not fast,</hi> because they did not proclaim their fasts. Note, We must not judge of people's religion by that which falls under the eye and observation of the world. But suppose it was so, that Christ's disciples did not <hi type="italic">fast</hi> so often or so long as they did, why truly, they would therefore have it thought, that they had more religion in them than Christ's disciples had. Note, It is common for vain professors to make themselves a standard in religion, by which to try and measure persons and things, as if all who differed from them were so far in the wrong; as if all that did less than they, did too little, and all that did more than they, did too much, which is a plain evidence of their want of humility and charity. <div eID="gen21898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21899" type="x-p"/> 3. How they brought this complaint to Christ. Note, If Christ's disciples, either by omission or commission, give offence, Christ himself will be sure to hear of it, and be reflected upon for it. <hi type="italic">O, Jesus, are these thy Christians?</hi> Therefore, as we tender the honour of Christ, we are concerned to conduct ourselves well. Observe, The quarrel with Christ was brought to the disciples (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.11">v. 11</reference>), the quarrel with the disciples was brought to Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.14">v. 14</reference>), this is the way of sowing discord and killing love, to set people against ministers, ministers against people, and one friend against another. <div eID="gen21899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21900" type="x-p"/> II. The apology which Christ made for his disciples in this matter. Christ might have upbraided John's disciples with the former part of their question, <hi type="italic">Why do ye fast often?</hi> "Nay, you know best why you do it; but the truth is, many abound in external instances of devotion, that scarcely do themselves know why and wherefore." But he only vindicates the practice of his disciples; whey they had nothing to say for themselves, he had something ready to say for them. Note, As it is wisdom's honour to be justified of all her children, so it is her children's happiness to be all justified of wisdom. What we do according to the precept and pattern of Christ, he will be sure to bear us out in, and we may with confidence leave it to him to clear up our integrity. <div eID="gen21900" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen21901"/> <l level="1" sID="gen21902"/><hi type="italic">But thou shalt answer, Lord, for me.</hi> Herbert.<l eID="gen21902" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen21901"/> <div sID="gen21903" type="x-p"/> Two things Christ pleads in defence of their <hi type="italic">not fasting.</hi> <div eID="gen21903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21904" type="x-p"/> 1. That it was not a season proper for that duty (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Can the children of the bride-chamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them?</hi> Observe, Christ's answer is so framed, as that it might sufficiently justify the practice of his own disciples, and yet not condemn the institution of John, or the practice of his disciples. When the Pharisees fomented this dispute, they hoped Christ would cast blame, either on his own disciples, or on John's, but he did neither. Note, When at any time we are unjustly censured, our care must be only to clear ourselves, not to recriminate, or throw dirt upon others; and such a variety may there be of circumstances, as may justify us in our practice, without condemning those that practise otherwise. <div eID="gen21904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21905" type="x-p"/> Now his argument is taken from the common usage of joy and rejoicing during the continuance of marriage solemnities; when all instances of melancholy and sorrow are looked upon as improper and absurd, as it was at Samson's wedding, <reference osisRef="Judg.14.17">Judges xiv. 17</reference>. Now, (1.) The disciples of Christ were the <hi type="italic">children of the bride-chamber,</hi> invited to the wedding-feast, and welcome there; the disciples of the Pharisees were not so, but <hi type="italic">children of the bond-woman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.25">Gal. iv. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.31">31</reference>), continuing under a dispensation of darkness and terror. Note, The faithful followers of Christ, who have the Spirit of adoption, have a continual feast, while they who have the spirit of bondage and fear, cannot rejoice for joy, as other people, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.1">Hos. ix. 1</reference>. (2.) The disciples of Christ had <hi type="italic">the bridegroom with them,</hi> which the disciples of John had not; their master was now cast into prison, and lay there in continual danger of his life, and therefore it was seasonable for them to <hi type="italic">fast often.</hi> Such a day would come upon the disciples of Christ, when the bridegroom should be taken from them, when they should be deprived of his bodily presence, and <hi type="italic">then should they fast.</hi> The thoughts of parting grieved them when he was going, <reference osisRef="John.16.6">John xvi. 6</reference>. Tribulation and affliction befel them when he was gone, and gave them occasion of <hi type="italic">mourning</hi> and <hi type="italic">praying,</hi> that is, of religious fasting. Note, [1.] Jesus Christ is the Bridegroom of his Church, and his disciples are the <hi type="italic">children of the bride-chamber.</hi> Christ speaks of himself to John's disciples under this similitude, because that John had used it, when he called himself a friend of the bridegroom, <reference osisRef="John.3.29">John iii. 29</reference>. And if they would by this hint call to mind what their master then said, they would answer themselves. [2.] The condition of those who are the children of the bride-chamber is liable to many changes and alterations in this world; they sing of mercy and judgment. [3.] It is merry or melancholy with the children of the bride-chamber, according as they have more or less of the bridegroom's presence. When he is with them, the candle of God shines upon their head, and all is well; but when he is withdrawn, though but for a small moment, <hi type="italic">they are troubled,</hi> and walk heavily; the presence and nearness of the sun makes day and summer, his absence and distance, night and winter. Christ is all in all to the church's joy. [4.] Every duty is to be done in its proper season. See <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Eccles. vii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">Jam. v. 13</reference>. There is a time to mourn and a time to laugh, to each of which we should accommodate ourselves, and bring forth fruit in due season. In fasts, regard is to be had to the methods of God's grace towards us; when he <hi type="italic">mourns to us,</hi> we must <hi type="italic">lament;</hi> and also to the dispensations of his providence concerning us; there are times when <hi type="italic">the Lord God calls to weeping and mourning;</hi> regard is likewise to be had to any special work before us, <reference osisRef="Matt.17.21">ch. xvii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.2">Acts xiii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen21905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21906" type="x-p"/> 2. That they had not strength sufficient for that duty. This is set forth in two similitudes, one of putting <hi type="italic">new cloth into an old garment,</hi> which does but pull the old to pieces (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.16">v. 16</reference>); the other of putting <hi type="italic">new wine into old bottles,</hi> which does but burst the bottles, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.17">v. 17</reference>. Christ's disciples were not able to bear these severe exercises so well as those of John and of the Pharisees, which the learned Dr. Whitby gives this reason for: There were among the Jews not only sects of the Pharisees and Essenes, who led an austere life, but also <hi type="italic">schools of the prophets,</hi> who frequently lived in mountains and deserts, and were many of them Nazarites; they had also private academies to train men up in a strict discipline; and possibly from these many of John's disciples might come, and many of the Pharisees; whereas Christ's disciples, being taken immediately from their callings, had not been used to such religious austerities, and were unfit for them, and would by them be rather unfitted for their other work. Note, (1.) Some duties of religion are harder and more difficult than others, like <hi type="italic">new cloth</hi> and <hi type="italic">new wine,</hi> which require most intenseness of mind, and are most displeasing to flesh and blood; such are religious fasting and the duties that attend it. (2.) The best of Christ's disciples pass through a state of infancy; all the trees in Christ's garden are not of a growth, nor all his scholars in the same form; there are <hi type="italic">babes in Christ</hi> and grown men. (3.) In the enjoining of religious exercises, the weakness and infirmity of young Christians ought to be considered: as the food provided for them must be such as is proper for their age (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.2">1 Cor. iii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.12">Heb. v. 12</reference>), so must the work be that is cut out for them. Christ would not speak to his disciples that which they could not then bear, <reference osisRef="John.16.12">John xvi. 12</reference>. Young beginners in religion must not be put upon the hardest duties at first, lest they be discouraged. Such as was God's care of his Israel, when he brought them out of Egypt, not to lead them by the way of the Philistines (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.17-Exod.13.18">Exod. xiii. 17, 18</reference>), and such as was Jacob's care of his children and cattle, not to overdrive them (<reference osisRef="Gen.33.13">Gen. xxxiii. 13</reference>), such is Christ's care of the little ones of his family, and the lambs of his flock: he gently leads them. For want of this care, many times, <hi type="italic">the bottles break,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the wine is spilled;</hi> the profession of many miscarries and comes to nothing, through indiscretion at first. Note, There may be <hi type="italic">over</hi>—doing even in <hi type="italic">well</hi>—doing, a being <hi type="italic">righteous over-much;</hi> and such an <hi type="italic">over</hi>—doing as may prove an <hi type="italic">un</hi>doing through the subtlety of Satan.
entries.d213387004334706a603ffb20ee81a8f1ec9a25e: <div eID="gen21906" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Ruler's Daughter Raised.</title> <div sID="gen21907" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> While he spake these things unto them, behold, there came a certain ruler, and worshipped him, saying, My daughter is even now dead: but come and lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Jesus arose, and followed him, and <hi type="italic">so did</hi> his disciples. <hi type="super">20</hi> And, behold, a woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and touched the hem of his garment: <hi type="super">21</hi> For she said within herself, If I may but touch his garment, I shall be whole. <hi type="super">22</hi> But Jesus turned him about, and when he saw her, he said, Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made thee whole. And the woman was made whole from that hour. <hi type="super">23</hi> And when Jesus came into the ruler's house, and saw the minstrels and the people making a noise, <hi type="super">24</hi> He said unto them, Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth. And they laughed him to scorn. <hi type="super">25</hi> But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose. <hi type="super">26</hi> And the fame hereof went abroad into all that land. <div eID="gen21907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21908" type="x-p"/> We have here two passages of history put together; that of the raising of Jairus's daughter to life, and that of the curing of the woman that had <hi type="italic">the bloody issue,</hi> as he was going to Jairus's house, which is introduced in a parenthesis, in the midst of the other; for Christ's miracles were thick sown, and interwoven; <hi type="italic">the work of him that sent</hi> him was his daily work. He was called to do these good works from speaking the things foregoing, in answer to the cavils of the Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">v. 18</reference>: <hi type="italic">While he spake these things;</hi> and we may suppose it is a pleasing interruption given to that unpleasant work of disputation, which, though sometimes needful, a good man will gladly leave, to go about a work of devotion or charity. Here is, <div eID="gen21908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21909" type="x-p"/> I. The ruler's address to Christ, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">A certain ruler,</hi> a ruler of the synagogue, <hi type="italic">came and worshipped him. Have any of the rulers believed on him?</hi> Yes, here was one, a church ruler, whose faith condemned the unbelief of the rest of the rulers. This ruler had a little daughter, of twelve years old, just dead, and this breach made upon his family comforts was the occasion of his coming to Christ. Note, In trouble we should visit God: the death of our relations should drive us to Christ, who is our life; it is well if any thing will do it. When affliction is in our families, we must not sit down astonished, but, as Job, <hi type="italic">fall down and worship.</hi> Now observe, <div eID="gen21909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21910" type="x-p"/> 1. His humility in this address to Christ. He came with his errand to Christ himself, and did not send his servant. Note, It is no disparagement to the greatest rulers, personally to attend on the Lord Jesus. He <hi type="italic">worshipped him,</hi> bowed the knee to him, and gave him all imaginable respect. Note, They that would receive mercy from Christ must give honour to Christ. <div eID="gen21910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21911" type="x-p"/> 2. His faith in this address; "<hi type="italic">My daughter is even now dead,</hi>" and though any other physician would now come too late (nothing more absurd than <hi type="italic">post mortem medicina—medicine after death</hi>), yet Christ comes not too late; he is a Physician after death, for he is <hi type="italic">the resurrection and the life;</hi> "<hi type="italic">O come</hi> then, <hi type="italic">and lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live.</hi>" This was quite above the power of nature (<hi type="italic">a privatione ad habitum non datur regressus—life once lost cannot be restored</hi>), yet within the power of Christ, who has <hi type="italic">life in himself, and quickeneth whom he will.</hi> Now Christ works in an ordinary, <hi type="italic">by</hi> nature and not <hi type="italic">against</hi> it, and, therefore, we cannot in faith bring him such a request as this; while there is life, there is hope, and room for prayer; but when our friends are dead, the case is determined; <hi type="italic">we shall go to them, but they shall not return to us.</hi> But while Christ was here upon earth working miracles, such a confidence as this was not only allowable but very commendable. <div eID="gen21911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21912" type="x-p"/> II. The readiness of Christ to comply with his address, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.19">v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi> immediately <hi type="italic">arose,</hi> left his company, <hi type="italic">and followed him;</hi> he was not only willing to grant him what he desired, in raising his daughter to life, but to gratify him so far as to come to his house to do it. Surely <hi type="italic">he never said to the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain.</hi> He denied to go along with the nobleman, who said, <hi type="italic">Sir, come down, ere my child die</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.48-John.4.50">John iv. 48-50</reference>), yet he went along with the ruler of the synagogue, who said, <hi type="italic">Sir, come down, and my child shall live.</hi> The variety of methods which Christ took in working his miracles is perhaps to be attributed to the different frame and temper of mind which they were in who applied to him, which he <hi type="italic">who searcheth the heart</hi> perfectly knew, and accommodated himself to. He knows what is in man, and what course to take with him. And observe, when <hi type="italic">Jesus followed him, so did his disciples,</hi> whom he had chosen for his constant companions; it was not for state, or that he might come with observation, that he took his attendants with him, but that they might be the witnesses of his miracles, who were hereafter to be the preachers of his doctrine. <div eID="gen21912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21913" type="x-p"/> III. The healing of the poor woman's bloody issue. I call her a poor woman, not only because her case was piteous, but because, she had <hi type="italic">spent it all upon physicians,</hi> for the cure of her distemper, and was never the better; which was a double aggravation of the misery of her condition, that she had been full, but was now empty; and that she had impoverished herself for the recovery of her health, and yet had not her health neither. This <hi type="italic">woman was diseased with a constant issue of blood twelve years</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.20">v. 20</reference>); a disease, which was not only weakening and wasting, and under which the body must needs languish; but which also rendered her ceremonially unclean, and shut her <hi type="italic">out from the courts of the Lord's house;</hi> but it did not cut her off from approaching to Christ. She applied herself to Christ, and received mercy from him, by the way, as he followed the ruler, whose daughter was dead, to whom it would be a great encouragement, and a help to keep up his faith in the power of Christ. So graciously does Christ consider the frame, and consult the case, of weak believers. Observe, <div eID="gen21913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21914" type="x-p"/> 1. The woman's great faith in Christ, and in his power. Her disease was of such a nature, that her modesty would not suffer her to speak openly to Christ for a cure, as others did, but by a peculiar impulse of the Spirit of faith, she believed him to have such an overflowing fulness of healing virtue, that the very <hi type="italic">touch of his garment</hi> would be her cure. This, perhaps, had something of fancy mixed with faith; for she had no precedent for this way of application to Christ, unless, as some think, she had an eye to the raising of the dead man by the touch of Elisha's bones, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.21">2 Kings xiii. 21</reference>. But what <hi type="italic">weakness of understanding</hi> there was in it, Christ was pleased to overlook, and to accept the sincerity and strength of her faith; for he <hi type="italic">eateth the honey-comb with the honey,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.11">Cant. iv. 11</reference>. She believed she should be healed if she did but <hi type="italic">touch the</hi> very <hi type="italic">hem of his garment,</hi> the very extremity of it. Note, There is virtue in every thing that belongs to Christ. The holy oil with which the high priest was anointed, <hi type="italic">ran down to the skirts of his garments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.133.2">Ps. cxxxiii. 2</reference>. Such a fulness of grace is there in Christ, that <hi type="italic">from it we may all receive,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen21914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21915" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ's great favour to this woman. He did not suspend (as he might have done) his healing influences, but suffered this bashful patient to steal a cure unknown to any one else, though she could not think to do it unknown to him. And now she was well content to be gone, for she had what she came for, but Christ was not willing to let he to so; he will not only have his power magnified in her cure, but his grace magnified in her comfort and commendation: the triumphs of her faith must be to her praise and honour. He <hi type="italic">turned about</hi> to see for her (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.22">v. 22</reference>), and soon discovered her. Note, It is great encouragement to humble Christians, that they who hide themselves from men are known to Christ, who sees in secret their applications to heaven when most private. Now here, <div eID="gen21915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21916" type="x-p"/> (1.) He <hi type="italic">puts gladness into her heart,</hi> by that word, <hi type="italic">Daughter, be of good comfort.</hi> She feared being chidden for coming clandestinely, but she is encouraged. [1.] He calls her <hi type="italic">daughter,</hi> for he spoke to her with the tenderness of a father, as he did <hi type="italic">to the man sick of the palsy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">v. 2</reference>), whom he called <hi type="italic">son.</hi> Note, Christ has comforts ready for <hi type="italic">the daughters of Zion,</hi> that are of a sorrowful spirit, as Hannah was, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.15">1 Sam. i. 15</reference>. Believing women are Christ's <hi type="italic">daughters,</hi> and he will own them as such. [2.] He bids her <hi type="italic">be of good comfort:</hi> she has reason to be so, if Christ own her for a <hi type="italic">daughter.</hi> Note, The saints' consolation is founded in their adoption. His bidding her <hi type="italic">be comforted,</hi> brought comfort with it, as his saying, <hi type="italic">Be ye whole,</hi> brought health with it. Note, It is the will of Christ that his people should be comforted, and it is his prerogative to command comfort to troubled spirits. He <hi type="italic">creates the fruit of the lips, peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Isa. lvii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen21916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21917" type="x-p"/> (2.) He puts honour upon her faith. That grace of all others gives most honour to Christ, and therefore he puts most honour upon it; <hi type="italic">Thy faith has made thee whole.</hi> Thus <hi type="italic">by faith she obtained a good report.</hi> And as of all graces Christ puts the greatest honour upon faith, so of all believers he puts the greatest honour upon those that are most humble; as here on this woman, who had more faith than she thought she had. She had reason to <hi type="italic">be of good comfort,</hi> not only because she was <hi type="italic">made whole,</hi> but because her <hi type="italic">faith had made her whole;</hi> that is, [1.] She was spiritually healed; that cure was wrought in her which is the proper fruit and effect of faith, the pardon of sin and the work of grace. Note, We may then be abundantly comforted in our temporal mercies when they are accompanied with those spiritual blessings that resemble them; our food and raiment will be comfortable, when by faith we are fed with <hi type="italic">the bread of life,</hi> and <hi type="italic">clothed with the righteousness of Jesus Christ;</hi> our rest and sleep will be comfortable, when by faith we repose in God, and dwell at ease in him; our health and prosperity will be comfortable, when by faith our souls prosper, and are in health. See <reference osisRef="Isa.38.16-Isa.38.17">Isa. xxxviii. 16, 17</reference>. [2.] Her bodily cure was the fruit of faith, of her faith, and that made it a happy, comfortable cure indeed. They out of whom the devils were cast, were helped by Christ's sovereign power; some by the faith of others (as <reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">v. 2</reference>); but it is <hi type="italic">thy faith that has made thee whole.</hi> Note, Temporal mercies are then comforts indeed to us, when they are received by faith. If, when in pursuit of mercy, we prayed for it in faith, with an eye to the promise, and in dependence upon that, if we desired it for the sake of God's glory, and with a resignation to God's will, and have our hearts enlarged by it in faith, love, and obedience, we may then say, it was received by faith. <div eID="gen21917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21918" type="x-p"/> IV. The posture in which he found the ruler's house, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.23">v. 23</reference>. —He <hi type="italic">saw the people and the minstrels,</hi> or musicians, <hi type="italic">making a noise.</hi> The house was in a hurry: such work does death make, when it comes into a family; and, perhaps, the necessary cares that arise at such a time, when our dead is to be decently buried out of our sight, give some useful diversion to that grief which is apt to prevail and play the tyrant. The people in the neighbourhood came together to condole on account of the loss, to comfort the parents, to prepare for, and attend on, the funeral, which the Jews were not wont to defer long. The musicians were among them, according to the custom of the Gentiles, with their doleful, melancholy tunes, to increase the grief, and stir up the lamentations of those that attended on this occasion; as (they say) is usual among the Irish, with their Ahone, Ahone. Thus they indulged a passion that is apt enough of itself to grow intemperate, and affected to <hi type="italic">sorrow as those that had no hope.</hi> See how religion provides cordials, where irreligion administers corrosives. Heathenism aggravates that grief which Christianity studies to assuage. Or perhaps these musicians endeavoured on the other hand to divert the grief and exhilarate the family; but, <hi type="italic">as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that sings songs to a heavy heart.</hi> Observe, The parents, who were immediately touched with the affliction, were silent, while <hi type="italic">the people and minstrels,</hi> whose lamentations were forced, made such a noise. Note, The loudest grief is not always the greatest; rivers are most noisy where they run shallow. <hi type="italic">Ille dolet vere, qui sine teste dolet—That grief is most sincere, which shuns observation.</hi> But notice is taken of this, to show that the girl was really dead, in the undoubted apprehension of all about her. <div eID="gen21918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21919" type="x-p"/> V. The rebuke that Christ gave to this hurry and noise, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.24">v. 24</reference>. He said, <hi type="italic">Give place.</hi> Note, Sometimes, when <hi type="italic">the sorrow of the world</hi> prevails, it is difficult for Christ and his comforts to enter. They that harden themselves in sorrow, and, like Rachel, <hi type="italic">refuse to be comforted,</hi> should think they hear Christ saying to their disquieting thoughts, <hi type="italic">Give place:</hi> "Make room for him who is <hi type="italic">the Consolation of Israel,</hi> and brings with him <hi type="italic">strong consolations,</hi> strong enough to overcome the confusion and tyranny of these worldly griefs, if he may but be admitted into the soul." He gives a good reason why they should not thus disquiet themselves and one another; <hi type="italic">The maid is not dead but sleepeth.</hi> 1. This was eminently true of this maid, that was immediately to be raised to life; she was really dead, but not so to Christ, who knew within himself what he would do, and could do, and who had determined to make her death but as a sleep. There is little more difference between sleep and death, but in continuance; whatever other difference there is, it is but a dream. This death must be but of short continuance, and therefore is but a sleep, like one night's rest. He that quickens the dead, may well call the things which be not as though they were, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.17">Rom. iv. 17</reference>. 2. It is in a sense true of all that die, chiefly of them <hi type="italic">that die in the Lord.</hi> Note, (1.) Death is a sleep. All nations and languages, for the softening of that which is so dreadful, and withal so unavoidable, and the reconciling of themselves to it, have agreed to call it so. It is said, even of the wicked kings, that they <hi type="italic">slept with their fathers;</hi> and of those that shall arise to everlasting contempt, that they <hi type="italic">sleep in the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan. xii. 2</reference>. It is not the sleep of the soul; its activity ceases not; but the sleep of the body, which lies down in the grave, still and silent, regardless and disregarded, wrapt up in darkness and obscurity. Sleep is a short death, and death a long sleep. But <hi type="italic">the death of the righteous</hi> is in a special manner to be looked upon as a sleep, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Isa. lvii. 2</reference>. They sleep in Jesus (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">1 Thess. iv. 14</reference>); they not only rest from the toils and labours of the day, but <hi type="italic">rest in hope</hi> of a joyful waking again in the morning of the resurrection, when they shall wake refreshed, wake to a new life, wake to be richly dressed and crowned, and <hi type="italic">wake to sleep no more.</hi> (2.) The consideration of this should moderate our grief at the death of our dear relations: "say not, They <hi type="italic">are</hi> lost; no, they are but <hi type="italic">gone before:</hi> say not, They are <hi type="italic">slain;</hi> no, they are but <hi type="italic">fallen asleep;</hi> and the apostle speaks of it as an absurd thing to imagine that <hi type="italic">they that are fallen asleep in Christ are perished</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.18">1 Cor. xv. 18</reference>); <hi type="italic">give place,</hi> therefore, to those comforts which the covenant of grace ministers, fetched from the future <hi type="italic">state, and the glory to be revealed.</hi>" <div eID="gen21919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21920" type="x-p"/> Now could it be thought that such a comfortable word as this, from the mouth of our Lord Jesus, should be ridiculed as it was? <hi type="italic">They laughed him to scorn.</hi> These people lived in Capernaum, knew Christ's character, that he never spake a rash or foolish word; they knew how many mighty works he had done; so that if they did not understand what he meant by this, they might at least have been silent in expectation of the issue. Note, The words and works of Christ which cannot be understood, yet are not therefore to be despised. We must adore the mystery of divine sayings, even when they seem to contradict what we think ourselves most confident of. Yet even this tended to the confirmation of the miracle: for it seems she was so apparently dead, that it was thought a very ridiculous thing to say otherwise. <div eID="gen21920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21921" type="x-p"/> VI. The raising of the damsel to life by the power of Christ, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.25">v. 25</reference>. <hi type="italic">The people were put forth.</hi> Note, Scorners that laugh at what they see and hear that is above their capacity, are not proper witnesses of the wonderful works of Christ, the glory of which lies not in pomp, but in power. The widow's son at Nain, and Lazarus, were raised from the dead openly, but this damsel privately; for Capernaum, that had slighted the lesser miracles of restoring health, was unworthy to see the greater, of restoring life; these <hi type="italic">pearls were not</hi> to be <hi type="italic">cast before</hi> those that would <hi type="italic">trample them under their feet.</hi> <div eID="gen21921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21922" type="x-p"/> Christ went in and <hi type="italic">took her by the hand,</hi> as it were to awake her, and to help her up, prosecuting his own metaphor of her being asleep. The high priest, that typified Christ, was not to come near the dead (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.10-Lev.21.11">Lev. xxi. 10, 11</reference>), but Christ <hi type="italic">touched the dead.</hi> The Levitical priesthood leaves the dead in their uncleanness, and therefore keeps at a distance from them, because it cannot remedy them; but Christ, having power to raise the dead, is above the infection, and therefore is not shy of touching them. He <hi type="italic">took her by the hand, and the maid arose.</hi> So easily, so effectually was the miracle wrought; not by prayer, as Elijah did (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.21">1 Kings xvii. 21</reference>), and Elisha (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.33">2 Kings iv. 33</reference>), but by a touch. They did it as servants, he as a Son, as a God, <hi type="italic">to whom belong the issues from death.</hi> Note, Jesus Christ is the Lord of souls, he commands them forth, and commands them back, when and as he pleases. Dead souls are not raised to spiritual life, unless Christ <hi type="italic">take them by the hand:</hi> it is done in the <hi type="italic">day of his power.</hi> He helps us up, or we lie still. <div eID="gen21922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21923" type="x-p"/> VII. The general notice that was taken of this miracle, though it was wrought privately; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.26">v. 26</reference>. <hi type="italic">The fame thereof went abroad into all that land:</hi> it was the common subject of discourse. Note, Christ's works are more talked of than considered and improved. And doubtless, they that heard only the report of Christ's miracles, were accountable for that as well as they that were eye-witnesses of them. Though we at this distance have not seen Christ's miracles, yet having an authentic history of them, we are bound, upon the credit of that, to receive his doctrine; and blessed <hi type="italic">are they that have not seen, and yet have believed,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.20.29">John xx. 29</reference>.
entries.c8977271317c16e91334591141f04f04d7efb11a: <div eID="gen21923" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Two Blind and a Dumb Man Healed.</title> <div sID="gen21924" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> And when Jesus departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, <hi type="italic">Thou</hi> Son of David, have mercy on us. <hi type="super">28</hi> And when he was come into the house, the blind men came to him: and Jesus saith unto them, Believe ye that I am able to do this? They said unto him, Yea, Lord. <hi type="super">29</hi> Then touched he their eyes, saying, According to your faith be it unto you. <hi type="super">30</hi> And their eyes were opened; and Jesus straitly charged them, saying, See <hi type="italic">that</hi> no man know <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">31</hi> But they, when they were departed, spread abroad his fame in all that country. <hi type="super">32</hi> As they went out, behold, they brought to him a dumb man possessed with a devil. <hi type="super">33</hi> And when the devil was cast out, the dumb spake: and the multitudes marvelled, saying, It was never so seen in Israel. <hi type="super">34</hi> But the Pharisees said, He casteth out devils through the prince of the devils. <div eID="gen21924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21925" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have an account of two more miracles wrought together by our Saviour. <div eID="gen21925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21926" type="x-p"/> I. The giving of sight to two blind men, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.27-Matt.9.31">v. 27-31</reference>. Christ is the Fountain of light as well as life; and as, by raising the dead, he showed himself to be the same that at first <hi type="italic">breathed into man the breath of life,</hi> so, by giving sight to the blind, he showed himself to be the same that at first <hi type="italic">commanded the light to shine out of darkness.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen21926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21927" type="x-p"/> 1. The importunate address of the blind men to Christ. He was returning from the ruler's house to his own lodgings, and these <hi type="italic">blind men followed him,</hi> as beggars do, with their incessant cries, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.27">v. 27</reference>. He that cured diseases so easily, so effectually, and, withal, at so cheap a rate, shall have patients enough. As for other things, so he is famed for an Oculist. Observe, <div eID="gen21927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21928" type="x-p"/> (1.) The title which these blind men gave to Christ; <hi type="italic">Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.</hi> The promise made to David, that of his loins the Messiah should come, was well known, and the Messiah was therefore commonly called <hi type="italic">the Son of David.</hi> At this time there was a general expectation of his appearing; these blind men know, and own, and proclaim it in the streets of Capernaum, that he is come, and that this is he; which aggravates the folly and sin of the chief priests and Pharisees who denied and opposed him. They could not see him and his miracles, but <hi type="italic">faith comes by hearing.</hi> Note, They who, by the providence of God, are deprived of bodily sight, may yet, by the grace of God, have <hi type="italic">the eyes of their understanding so enlightened,</hi> as to discern those great things of God, <hi type="italic">which are hid from the wise and prudent.</hi> <div eID="gen21928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21929" type="x-p"/> (2.)
