Their petition, <hi type="italic">Have mercy on us.</hi> It was foretold that the <hi type="italic">Son of David</hi> should be <hi type="italic">merciful</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.12-Ps.72.13">Ps. lxxii. 12, 13</reference>), and in him <hi type="italic">shines the tender mercy of our God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.78">Luke i. 78</reference>. Note, Whatever our necessities and burthens are, we need no more for supply and support, than a share in the <hi type="italic">mercy of our Lord Jesus.</hi> Whether he heal us or no, if he <hi type="italic">have mercy on us,</hi> we have enough; as to the particular instances and methods of mercy, we may safely and wisely refer ourselves to the wisdom of Christ. They did not each of them say for himself, <hi type="italic">Have mercy on me,</hi> but both for one another, <hi type="italic">Have mercy on us.</hi> Note, It becomes those that are under the same affliction, to concur in the same prayers for relief. Fellow-sufferers should be joint-petitioners. In Christ there is enough for all. <div eID="gen21929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21930" type="x-p"/> (3.) Their importunity in this request; they <hi type="italic">followed him, crying.</hi> It seems, he did not take notice of them at first, for he would try their faith, which he knew to be strong; would quicken their prayers, and make his cures the more valued, when they did not always come at the first word; and would teach us to <hi type="italic">continue instant in prayer, always to pray, and not to faint:</hi> and, though the answer do not come presently, yet to wait for it, and to follow providence, even in those steps and out goings of it which seem to neglect or contradict our prayers. Christ would not heal them publicly in the streets, for this was a cure he would have kept private (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.30">v. 30</reference>), but <hi type="italic">when he came into the house,</hi> they <hi type="italic">followed him</hi> thither, and <hi type="italic">came to him.</hi> Note, Christ's doors are always open to believing and importunate petitioners; it seemed rude in them to rush into the house after him, when he desired to retire; but, such is the tenderness of our Lord Jesus, that they were not more bold than welcome. <div eID="gen21930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21931" type="x-p"/> 2. The confession of faith, which Christ drew from them upon this occasion. When they came to him for mercy, he asked them, <hi type="italic">Believe ye that I am able to do this?</hi> Note, Faith is the great condition of Christ's favours. They who would receive the <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> of Christ, must firmly believe the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of Christ. What we would have him do for us, we must be fully assured that he is <hi type="italic">able to do.</hi> They followed Christ, and followed him crying, but the great question is, <hi type="italic">Do ye believe?</hi> Nature may work fervency, but it is only grace that can work faith; spiritual blessings are obtained only by faith. They had intimated their faith in the office of Christ as <hi type="italic">Son of David,</hi> and in his mercy; but Christ demands likewise a profession of faith in his power. <hi type="italic">Believe ye that I am able to do this;</hi> to bestow this favour; to give sight to the blind, as well as to cure the palsy and raise the dead? Note, It is good to be particular in the exercise of faith, to apply the general assurances of God's power and good will, and the general promises, to our particular exigencies. <hi type="italic">All shall work for good,</hi> and if all, then this. "<hi type="italic">Believe ye that I am able,</hi> not only to prevail with God for it, as a prophet, but <hi type="italic">that I am able to do it</hi> by my own power?" This will amount to their belief of his being not only <hi type="italic">the Son of David,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the Son of God;</hi> for it is God's prerogative to <hi type="italic">open the eyes of the blind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.8">Ps. cxlvi. 8</reference>); he makes <hi type="italic">the seeing eye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.4.11">Exod. iv. 11</reference>. Job <hi type="italic">was eyes to the blind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.29.15">Job xxix. 15</reference>); was to them instead of eyes, but he could not <hi type="italic">give</hi> eyes to the blind. Still it is put to us, <hi type="italic">Believe we that Christ is able to do for us,</hi> by the power of his merit and intercession in heaven, of his Spirit and grace in the heart, and of his providence and dominion in the world? To believe the power of Christ is not only to assure ourselves of it, but to commit ourselves to it, and encourage ourselves in it. <div eID="gen21931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21932" type="x-p"/> To this question they give an immediate answer, without hesitation: they said, <hi type="italic">Yea, Lord.</hi> Though he had kept them in suspense awhile, and had not helped them at first, they honestly imputed that to his wisdom, not to his weakness, and were still confident of his ability. Note, The treasures of mercy that are laid up in the power of Christ, are <hi type="italic">laid out and wrought for those that trust in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.31.19">Ps. xxxi. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen21932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21933" type="x-p"/> 3. The cure that Christ wrought on them; <hi type="italic">he touched their eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.9.29">v. 29</reference>. This he did to encourage their faith, which, by his delay, he had tried, and to show that he gives sight to blind souls by the operations of his grace accompanying the word, <hi type="italic">anointing the eyes with eye-salve:</hi> and he put the cure upon their faith, <hi type="italic">According to your faith be it unto you.</hi> When they begged for a cure, he enquired into their faith (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.28">v. 28</reference>), <hi type="italic">Believe ye that I am able?</hi> He did not enquire into their wealth, whether they were able to pay him for a cure; nor into their reputation, should he get credit by curing them; but into their faith; and now they had professed their faith he referred the matter to that: "I know you do believe, and the power you believe in shall be exerted for you; <hi type="italic">According to your faith be it unto you.</hi>" This speaks, (1.) His knowledge of the sincerity of their faith, and his acceptance and approbation of it. Note, It is a great comfort to true believers, that Jesus Christ knows their faith, and is well pleased with it. Though it be weak, though others do not discern it, though they themselves are ready to question it, it is known to him. (2.) His insisting upon their faith as necessary; "If you believe, take what you come for." Note, They who apply themselves to Jesus Christ, shall be dealt with <hi type="italic">according to their faith;</hi> not according to their <hi type="italic">fancies,</hi> nor according to their <hi type="italic">profession,</hi> but <hi type="italic">according to their faith;</hi> that is, unbelievers cannot expect to find any favour with God, but true believers may be sure to find all that favour which is offered in the gospel; and our comforts ebb or flow, according as our faith is stronger or weaker; we are not straitened in Christ, let us not then be straitened in ourselves. <div eID="gen21933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21934" type="x-p"/> 4. The charge he gave them to keep it private (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.30">v. 30</reference>), <hi type="italic">See that no man know it.</hi> He gave them this charge, (1.) To set us an example of that humility and lowliness of mind, which he would have us to learn of him. Note, In the good we do, we must not seek our own praise, but only the glory of God. It must be more our care and endeavour to be useful, than to be known and observed to be so, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.6">Prov. xx. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.27">xxv. 27</reference> Thus Christ seconded the rule he had given, <hi type="italic">Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth.</hi> (2.) Some think that Christ, in keeping it private, showed his displeasure against the people of Capernaum, who had seen so many miracles, and yet believed not. Note, The silencing of those who should proclaim the works of Christ is a judgment to any place or people: and it is just in Christ to deny the means of conviction to those that are obstinate in their infidelity; and to shroud the light from those that shut their eyes against it. (3.) He did it in discretion, for his own preservation; because the more he was proclaimed, the more jealous would the rulers of the Jews be of his growing interest among the people. (4.) Dr. Whitby gives another reason, which is very considerable, why Christ sometimes concealed his miracles, and afterwards forbid the publishing of his transfiguration; because he would not indulge that pernicious conceit which obtained among the Jews, that their Messiah should be a temporal prince, and so give occasion to the people to attempt the setting up of his kingdom, by tumults and seditions, as they offered to do, <reference osisRef="John.6.15">John vi. 15</reference>. But when, after his resurrection (which was the full proof of his mission), his spiritual kingdom was set up, then that danger was over, and they must be published to all nations. And he observes, that the miracles which Christ wrought among the Gentiles and the Gadarenes, were ordered to be published, because with them there was not that danger. <div eID="gen21934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21935" type="x-p"/> But honour is like the shadow, which, as it flees from those that follow it, so it follows those that flee from it (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.31">v. 31</reference>); <hi type="italic">They spread abroad his fame.</hi> This was more an act of zeal, than of prudence; and though it may be excused as honestly meant for the honour of Christ, yet it cannot be justified, being done against a particular charge. Whenever we profess to direct our intention to the glory of God, we must see to it that the action be according to the will of God. <div eID="gen21935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21936" type="x-p"/> II. The healing of a <hi type="italic">dumb man,</hi> that was <hi type="italic">possessed with a devil.</hi> And here observe, <div eID="gen21936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21937" type="x-p"/> 1. His case, which was very sad. He was under the power of the devil in this particular instance, that he was disabled from speaking, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.32">v. 32</reference>. See the calamitous state of this world, and how various the afflictions of the afflicted are! We have no sooner dismissed <hi type="italic">two blind men,</hi> but we meet with a <hi type="italic">dumb man.</hi> How thankful should we be to God for our sight and speech! See the malice of Satan against mankind, and in how many ways he shows it. This man's dumbness was the effect of his being <hi type="italic">possessed with a devil;</hi> but it was better he should be unable to say any thing, than be forced to say, as those demoniacs did (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.29">ch. viii. 29</reference>), <hi type="italic">What have we to do with thee?</hi> Of the two, better a dumb devil than a blaspheming one. When the devil gets possession of a soul, it is made silent as to any thing that is good; dumb in prayers and praises, which the devil is a sworn enemy to. This poor creature <hi type="italic">they brought to Christ,</hi> who entertained not only those that came of themselves in their own faith, but those that were <hi type="italic">brought to him</hi> by their friends in the faith of others. Though <hi type="italic">the just shall live</hi> eternally <hi type="italic">by his faith,</hi> yet temporal mercies may be bestowed on us with an eye to their faith who are intercessors on our behalf. They brought him in just as <hi type="italic">the blind man went out.</hi> See how unwearied Christ was in doing good; how closely one good work followed another! Treasures of mercy, wondrous mercy, are hid in him; which may be continually communicated, but can never be exhausted. <div eID="gen21937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21938" type="x-p"/> 2. His cure, which was very sudden (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.33">v. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">When the devil was cast out, the dumb spake.</hi> Note, Christ's cures strike at the root, and remove the effect by taking away the cause; they open the lips, by breaking Satan's power in the soul. In sanctification he heals the waters by casting salt into the spring. When Christ, by his grace, <hi type="italic">casts the devil out</hi> of a soul, presently <hi type="italic">the dumb speaks.</hi> When Paul was converted, <hi type="italic">behold, he prays;</hi> then <hi type="italic">the dumb spake.</hi> <div eID="gen21938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21939" type="x-p"/> 3. The consequences of this cure. <div eID="gen21939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21940" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">The multitudes marvelled;</hi> and well they might; though <hi type="italic">few believed, many wondered.</hi> The admiration of the common people is sooner raised than any other affection. It was foretold, that the new song, the New-Testament song, should be sung for <hi type="italic">marvellous works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Ps. xcviii. 1</reference>. They said, <hi type="italic">It was never so seen in Israel,</hi> and therefore never so seen any where; for no people experienced such wonders of mercy as Israel did. There had been those in Israel that were famous for working miracles, but Christ excelled them all. The miracles Moses wrought had reference to Israel as a people, but Christ's were brought home to particular persons. <div eID="gen21940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21941" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">The Pharisees</hi> blasphemed, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.34">v. 34</reference>. When they could not gainsay the convincing evidence of these miracles, they fathered them upon the devil, as if they had been wrought by compact and collusion: <hi type="italic">he casteth out devils</hi> (say they) by <hi type="italic">the prince of the devils</hi>—a suggestion horrid beyond expression; we shall hear more of it afterwards, and Christ's answer to it (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.25">ch. xii. 25</reference>); only observe here, how <hi type="italic">evil men and seducers wax worse and worse</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.13">2 Tim. iii. 13</reference>), and it is both their sin and their punishment. Their quarrels with Christ for taking upon him to <hi type="italic">forgive sin</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.3">v. 3</reference>), for <hi type="italic">conversing with publicans and sinners,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.11">v. 11</reference>), for <hi type="italic">not fasting</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.14">v. 14</reference>), though spiteful enough, yet had some colour of piety, purity, and devotion in them; but this (which they are left to, to punish them for those) breathes nothing but malice and falsehood, and hellish enmity in the highest degree; it is diabolism all over, and was therefore justly pronounced unpardonable. Because the people marvelled, they must say something to diminish the miracle, and this was all they could say.
entries.27588d97d5dbc5db9af792fd65300320906f5d0b: <div eID="gen21941" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jesus Preaching throughout the Country.</title> <div sID="gen21942" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease among the people. <hi type="super">36</hi> But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd. <hi type="super">37</hi> Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly <hi type="italic">is</hi> plenteous, but the labourers <hi type="italic">are</hi> few; <hi type="super">38</hi> Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest. <div eID="gen21942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21943" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A conclusion of the foregoing account of Christ's preaching and miracles (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.35">v. 35</reference>); <hi type="italic">He went about all the cities teaching and healing.</hi> This is the same we had before, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.23">ch. iv. 23</reference>. There it ushers in the more particular record of Christ's preaching (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.1-Matt.7.29">ch. v., vi. and vii.</reference>) and of his cures (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.1-Matt.9.38">ch. viii. and ix.</reference>), and here it is elegantly repeated in the close of these instances, as the <hi type="italic">quod erat demonstrandum—the point to be proved;</hi> as if the evangelist should say, "Now I hope I have made it out, by an induction of particulars, that Christ preached and healed; for you have had the heads of his sermons, and some few instances of his cures, which were wrought to confirm his doctrine: and <hi type="italic">these were written that you might believe.</hi>" Some think that this was a second perambulation in Galilee, like the former; he visited again those whom he had before preached to. Though the Pharisees cavilled at him and opposed him, he went on with his work; he <hi type="italic">preached the gospel of the kingdom.</hi> He told them of a kingdom of grace and glory, now to be set up under the government of a Mediator: this was gospel indeed, <hi type="italic">good news, glad tidings of great joy.</hi> <div eID="gen21943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21944" type="x-p"/> Observe how Christ in his preaching had respect, <div eID="gen21944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21945" type="x-p"/> 1. To the private towns. He visited not only the great and wealthy cities, but the poor, obscure villages; there he preached, there he healed. The souls of those that are meanest in the world are as precious to Christ, and should be to us, as the souls of those that make the greatest figure. <hi type="italic">Rich and poor meet together</hi> in him, citizens and boors: his <hi type="italic">righteous acts towards the inhabitants of his villages</hi> must be <hi type="italic">rehearsed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.5.11">Judg. v. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen21945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21946" type="x-p"/> 2. To the public worship. He taught <hi type="italic">in their synagogues,</hi> (1.) That he might bear a testimony to solemn assemblies, even then when there were corruptions in them. We <hi type="italic">must not forsake the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is.</hi> (2.) That he might have an opportunity of preaching there, where people were gathered together, with an expectation to hear. Thus, even where the gospel church was founded, and Christian meetings erected, the apostles often <hi type="italic">preached in the synagogues of the Jews.</hi> It is the wisdom of the prudent, to make the best of that which is. <div eID="gen21946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21947" type="x-p"/> II. A preface, or introduction, to the account in the following chapter, of his sending forth his apostles. <hi type="italic">He</hi> took notice of <hi type="italic">the multitude</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.36">v. 36</reference>); not only of the crowds that <hi type="italic">followed him,</hi> but of the vast numbers of people with whom (as he passed along) he observed the country to be replenished; he noticed what nests of souls the towns and cities were, and how thick of inhabitants; what abundance of people there were in every synagogue, and what places of concourse the openings of the gates were: so very populous was that nation now grown; and it was the effect of God's blessing on Abraham. Seeing this, <div eID="gen21947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21948" type="x-p"/> 1. He pities them, and was concerned for them (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.36">v. 36</reference>); <hi type="italic">He was moved with compassion on them;</hi> not upon a temporal account, as he pities the blind, and lame, and sick; but upon a spiritual account; he was concerned to see them ignorant and careless, and ready to perish for lack of vision. Note, Jesus Christ is a very compassionate friend to precious souls; here his bowels do in a special manner yearn. It was pity to souls that brought him from heaven to earth, and there to the cross. Misery is the object of mercy; and the miseries of sinful, self-destroying souls, are the greatest miseries: Christ pities those most that pity themselves least; so should we. The most Christian compassion is compassion to souls; it is most Christ-like. <div eID="gen21948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21949" type="x-p"/> See what moved this pity. (1.) <hi type="italic">They fainted;</hi> they were destitute, vexed, wearied. <hi type="italic">They strayed,</hi> so some; were loosed one from another; <hi type="italic">The staff of bands was broken,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.11.14">Zech. xi. 14</reference>. They wanted help for their souls, and had none at hand that was good for any thing. The scribes and Pharisees filled them with vain notions, burthened them with the traditions of the elders, deluded them into many mistakes, while they were not instructed in their duty, nor acquainted with the extent and spiritual nature of the divine law; therefore <hi type="italic">they fainted;</hi> for what spiritual health, and life, and vigour can there be in those souls, that are fed with husks and ashes, instead of <hi type="italic">the bread of life?</hi> Precious souls <hi type="italic">faint</hi> when duty is to be done, temptations to be resisted, afflictions to be borne, being not nourished up with the word of truth. (2.) <hi type="italic">They were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.</hi> That expression is borrowed from <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.17">1 Kings xxii. 17</reference>, and it sets forth the sad condition of those that are destitute of faithful guides to go before them in the things of God. No creature is more apt to go astray than a sheep, and when gone astray more helpless, shiftless, and exposed, or more unapt to find the way home again: sinful souls <hi type="italic">are as lost sheep;</hi> they need the care of shepherds to bring them back. The teachers the Jews then had pretended to be <hi type="italic">shepherds,</hi> yet Christ says they had not <hi type="italic">shepherds,</hi> for they were worse than none; idle shepherds that led them away, instead of leading them back, and fleeced the flock, instead of feeding it: such shepherds as were described, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.1">Jer. xxiii. 1,</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.2">Ezek. xxxiv. 2</reference>, &c. Note, The case of those people is very pitiable, who either have no ministers at all, or those that are as bad as none; that seek their own things, not <hi type="italic">the things of Christ</hi> and souls. <div eID="gen21949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21950" type="x-p"/> 2. He excited his disciples to pray for them. His pity put him upon devising means for the good of these people. It appears (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.12-Luke.6.13">Luke vi. 12, 13</reference>) that upon this occasion, before he sent out his apostles, he did himself spend a great deal of time in prayer. Note, Those we pity we should pray for. Having spoken to God for them he turns to his disciples, and tells them, <div eID="gen21950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21951" type="x-p"/> (1.) How the case stood; <hi type="italic">The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few.</hi> People desired good preaching, but there were few good preachers. There was a great deal of work to be done, and a great deal of good likely to be done, but there wanted hands to do it. [1.] It was an encouragement, that <hi type="italic">the harvest</hi> was so <hi type="italic">plenteous.</hi> It was not strange, that there were multitudes that needed instruction, but it was what does not often happen, that they who needed it, desired it, and were forward to receive it. They that were ill taught were desirous to be better taught; people's expectations were raised, and there was such a moving of affections, as promised well. Note, It is a blessed thing, to see people in love with good preaching. The valleys are then covered over with corn, and there are hopes it may be well gathered in. That is a gale of opportunity, that calls for a double care and diligence in the improvement of it; a harvest-day should be a busy day. [2.] It was a pity when it was so that <hi type="italic">the labourers</hi> should be so <hi type="italic">few;</hi> that the corn should shed and spoil, and rot upon the ground for want of reapers; loiterers many, but <hi type="italic">labourers</hi> very <hi type="italic">few.</hi> Note, It is ill with the church, when good work stands still, or goes slowly on, for want of good workmen; when it is so, the <hi type="italic">labourers</hi> that there are have need to be very busy. <div eID="gen21951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21952" type="x-p"/> (2.) What was their duty in this case (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.38">v. 38</reference>); <hi type="italic">Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest.</hi> Note, The melancholy aspect of the times and the deplorable state of precious souls, should much excite and quicken prayer. When things look discouraging, we should pray more, and then we should complain and fear less. And we should adapt our prayers to the present exigencies of the church; such an understanding we ought to have of the times, as to know, not only what Israel ought to do, but what Israel ought to pray for. Note, [1.] God is <hi type="italic">the Lord of the harvest; my Father is the Husbandman,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.1">John xv. 1</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">the vineyard of the Lord of hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.5.7">Isa. v. 7</reference>. It is for him and to him, and to his service and honour, that <hi type="italic">the harvest</hi> is gathered in. <hi type="italic">Ye are God's husbandry</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">1 Cor. iii. 9</reference>); <hi type="italic">his threshing, and the corn of his floor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Isa. xxi. 10</reference>. He orders every thing concerning <hi type="italic">the harvest</hi> as he pleases; when and where <hi type="italic">the labourers</hi> shall work, and how long; and it is very comfortable to those who wish well to <hi type="italic">the harvest-work,</hi> that God himself presides in it, who will be sure to order all for the best. [2.] Ministers are and should be <hi type="italic">labourers</hi> in God's <hi type="italic">harvest;</hi> the ministry is a <hi type="italic">work</hi> and must be attended to accordingly; it is <hi type="italic">harvest-work,</hi> which is needful work; work that requires every thing to be done in its season, and diligence to do it thoroughly; but it is pleasant work; they <hi type="italic">reap in joy,</hi> and the joy of the preachers of the gospel is likened to the <hi type="italic">joy of harvest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.2-Isa.9.3">Isa. ix. 2, 3</reference>); and <hi type="italic">he that reapeth receiveth wages; the hire of the labourers</hi> that reap down God's field, shall not be <hi type="italic">kept back,</hi> as theirs was, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jam. v. 4</reference>. [3.] It is God's work to <hi type="italic">send forth labourers;</hi> Christ makes ministers (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">Eph. iv. 11</reference>); the office is of his appointing, the qualifications of his working, the call of his giving. They will not be owned nor paid as <hi type="italic">labourers,</hi> that run without their errand, unqualified, uncalled. <hi type="italic">How shall they preach except they be sent?</hi> [4.] All that love Christ and souls, should show it by their earnest prayers to God, especially when <hi type="italic">the harvest is plenteous, that he would send forth</hi> more skillful, faithful, wise, and industrious <hi type="italic">labourers into his harvest;</hi> that he would raise up such as he will own in the conversion of sinners and the edification of saints; would give them a spirit for the work, call them to it, and succeed them in it; <hi type="italic">that he would</hi> give them <hi type="italic">wisdom to win souls; that he would thrust forth labourers,</hi> so some; intimating unwillingness to go forth, because of their own weakness and the people's badness, and opposition from men, that endeavour to thrust them out of <hi type="italic">the harvest;</hi> but we should pray that all contradiction from within and from without, may be conquered and got over. Christ puts his friends upon praying this, just before he sends apostles forth to labour in <hi type="italic">the harvest.</hi> Note, It is a good sign God is about to bestow some special mercy upon a people, when he stirs up those that have an interest at the throne of grace, to pray for it, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Ps. x. 17</reference>. Further observe, that Christ said this to his disciples, who were to be employed as <hi type="italic">labourers.</hi> They must pray, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That God <hi type="italic">would send them forth. Here am I, send me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.6.8">Isa. vi. 8</reference>. Note, Commissions, given in answer to prayer, are most likely to be successful; Paul is a chosen vessel, for <hi type="italic">behold he prays,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.9.11">Acts ix. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.15">15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That he would send others forth. Note, Not the people only, but those who are themselves ministers, should pray for the increase of ministers. Though self-interest makes those that seek their own things desirous to be placed alone (the fewer ministers the more preferments), yet those that <hi type="italic">seek the things of Christ,</hi> desire more workmen, that more work may be done, though they be eclipsed by it.  <chapter eID="Matt.9"/> <div eID="gen21952" type="x-p"/>

entries.d0dba304dfbe5b288d53c72eea73b3e072d25333: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13468"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.9.1-Matt.9.8">Mt 9:1-8</reference>. Healing of a Paralytic. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.2.1-Mark.2.12">Mr 2:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.5.17-Luke.5.26">Lu 5:17-26</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25729" type="x-p"/> This incident appears to follow next in order of time to the cure of the leper (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.1-Matt.8.4">Mt 8:1-4</reference>). For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.2.1-Mark.2.12">Mr 2:1-12</reference>.<div eID="gen25729" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.9.9-Matt.9.13">Mt 9:9-13</reference>. Matthew's Call and Feast. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.2.14-Mark.2.17">Mr 2:14-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.5.27-Luke.5.32">Lu 5:27-32</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25730" type="x-p"/> The Call of Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.9">Mt 9:9</reference>).<div eID="gen25730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25731" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13468"/><hi type="bold">9. And as Jesus passed forth from thence--</hi>that is, from the scene of the paralytic's cure in Capernaum, towards the shore of the Sea of Galilee, on which that town lay. Mark, as usual, pictures the scene more in detail, thus (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.13">Mr 2:13</reference>): "And He went forth again by the seaside; and all the multitude resorted unto Him, and He taught them"--or, "kept teaching them." "And as He passed by"<div eID="gen25731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25732" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he saw a man, named Matthew--</hi>the writer of this precious Gospel, who here, with singular modesty and brevity, relates the story of his own calling. In Mark and Luke he is called Levi, which seems to have been his family name. In their lists of the twelve apostles, however, Mark and Luke give him the name of Matthew, which seems to have been the name by which he was known as a disciple. While he himself sinks his family name, he is careful not to sink his occupation, the obnoxious associations with which he would place over against the grace that called him from it, and made him an apostle. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.3">Mt 10:3</reference>). Mark alone tells us (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.14">Mr 2:14</reference>) that he was "the son of Alphæus"--the same, probably, with the father of James the Less. From this and other considerations it is pretty certain that he must at least have heard of our Lord before this meeting. Unnecessary doubts, even from an early period, have been raised about the identity of Levi and Matthew. No capable jury, with the evidence before them which we have in the Gospels, would hesitate in giving a unanimous verdict of identity.<div eID="gen25732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sitting at the receipt of custom--</hi>as a publican, which Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.27">Lu 5:27</reference>) calls him. It means the place of receipt, the toll house or booth in which the collector sat. Being in this case by the seaside, it might be the ferry tax for the transit of persons and goods across the lake, which he collected. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.5.46">Mt 5:46</reference>).<div eID="gen25733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he saith unto him, Follow me--</hi>Witching words these, from the lips of Him who never employed them without giving them resistless efficacy in the hearts of those they were spoken to.<div eID="gen25734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And he--</hi>"left all" (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.28">Lu 5:28</reference>), "arose and followed him."<div eID="gen25735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25736" type="x-p"/> The Feast (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.10-Matt.9.13">Mt 9:10-13</reference>). <div eID="gen25736" type="x-p"/>
entries.e872f99cdf94ee0effa179a7ebbb55f338a3136c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13469"/><div sID="gen25737" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13469"/><hi type="bold">10. And it came to pass, as Jesus sat at meat in the house--</hi>The modesty of our Evangelist signally appears here. Luke says (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.29">Lu 5:29</reference>) that "Levi made Him a great feast," or "reception," while Matthew merely says, "He sat at meat"; and Mark and Luke say that it was in Levi's "own house," while Matthew merely says, "He sat at meat in the house." Whether this feast was made now, or not till afterwards, is a point of some importance in the order of events, and not agreed among harmonists. The probability is that it did not take place till a considerable time afterwards. For Matthew, who ought surely to know what took place while his Lord was speaking at his own table, tells us that the visit of Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, occurred at that moment (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">Mt 9:18</reference>). But we know from Mark and Luke that this visit of Jairus did not take place till after our Lord's return, at a later period from the country of the Gadarenes. (See <reference osisRef="Mark.5.21">Mr 5:21</reference>, &c., and <reference osisRef="Luke.8.40">Lu 8:40</reference>, &c.). We conclude, therefore, that the feast was not made in the novelty of his discipleship, but after Matthew had had time to be somewhat established in the faith; when returning to Capernaum, his compassion for old friends, of his own calling and character, led him to gather them together that they might have an opportunity of hearing the gracious words which proceeded out of His Master's mouth, if haply they might experience a like change.<div eID="gen25737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25738" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold, many publicans and sinners--</hi>Luke says, "a great company" (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.29">Lu 5:29</reference>)<div eID="gen25738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came and sat down with him and his disciples--</hi>In all such cases the word rendered "sat" is "reclined," in allusion to the ancient mode of lying on couches at meals. <div eID="gen25739" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a8530d6e12c502b4549b55897713d1454f15bb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13470"/><div sID="gen25740" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13470"/><hi type="bold">11. And when the Pharisees--</hi>"and scribes," add Mark and Luke (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.6">Mr 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.5.21">Lu 5:21</reference>).<div eID="gen25740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saw it, they said--</hi>"murmured" or "muttered," says Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.30">Lu 5:30</reference>).<div eID="gen25741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto his disciples--</hi>not venturing to put their question to Jesus Himself.<div eID="gen25742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.15.2">Lu 15:2</reference>). <div eID="gen25743" type="x-p"/>
entries.810f1bd5c71c46984bb44fd81c4e90dd5c8d702c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13471"/><div sID="gen25744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13471"/><hi type="bold">12. But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them--</hi>to the Pharisees and scribes; addressing Himself to them, though they had shrunk from addressing Him.<div eID="gen25744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick--</hi>that is, "Ye deem yourselves whole; My mission, therefore, is not to you: The physician's business is with the sick; therefore eat I with publicans and sinners." Oh, what myriads of broken hearts, of sin-sick souls, have been bound up by this matchless saying! <div eID="gen25745" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab46149abf1388e3cea05d8faf1d97d363ab56a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13472"/><div sID="gen25746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13472"/><hi type="bold">13. But go ye and learn what that meaneth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Ho 6:6</reference>),<div eID="gen25746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will have mercy, and not sacrifice--</hi>that is, the one rather than the other. "Sacrifice," the chief part of the ceremonial law, is here put for a religion of literal adherence to mere rules; while "mercy" expresses such compassion for the fallen as seeks to lift them up. The duty of keeping aloof from the polluted, in the sense of "having no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness," is obvious enough; but to understand this as prohibiting such intercourse with them as is necessary to their recovery, is to abuse it. This was what these pharisaical religionists did, and this is what our Lord here exposes.<div eID="gen25747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance--</hi>The italicized words are of doubtful authority here, and more than doubtful authority in <reference osisRef="Mark.2.17">Mr 2:17</reference>; but in <reference osisRef="Luke.5.32">Lu 5:32</reference> they are undisputed. We have here just the former statement stripped of its figure. "The righteous" are the whole; "sinners," the sick. When Christ "called" the latter, as He did Matthew, and probably some of those publicans and sinners whom he had invited to meet Him, it was to heal them of their spiritual maladies, or save their souls: "The righteous," like those miserable self-satisfied Pharisees, "He sent empty away."<div eID="gen25748" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.9.14-Matt.9.17">Mt 9:14-17</reference>. Discourse on Fasting.</title> <div sID="gen25749" type="x-p"/> See on <reference osisRef="Luke.5.33-Luke.5.39">Lu 5:33-39</reference>.<div eID="gen25749" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.9.18-Matt.9.26">Mt 9:18-26</reference>. The Woman with the Issue of Blood Healed.--The Daughter of Jairus Raised to Life. ( = <reference osisRef="Luke.8.40-Luke.8.56">Lu 8:40-56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.5.21-Mark.5.43">Mr 5:21-43</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25750" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.5.21-Mark.5.43">Mr 5:21-43</reference>.<div eID="gen25750" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.9.27-Matt.9.34">Mt 9:27-34</reference>. Two Blind Men and a Dumb Demoniac Healed.</title> <div sID="gen25751" type="x-p"/> These two miracles are recorded by Matthew alone.<div eID="gen25751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25752" type="x-p"/> Two Blind Men Healed (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.27-Matt.9.31">Mt 9:27-31</reference>). <div eID="gen25752" type="x-p"/>
entries.e545bf6c19d0b3323f2ae42809226f48fbbb44a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13473"/><div sID="gen25753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13473"/><hi type="bold">27. And when Jesus departed thence, two blind men followed him--</hi>hearing, doubtless, as in a later case is expressed, "that Jesus passed by" (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.30">Mt 20:30</reference>).<div eID="gen25753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crying, and saying, Thou son of David, have mercy on us--</hi>It is remarkable that in the only other recorded case in which the blind applied to Jesus for their sight, and obtained it, they addressed Him, over and over again, by this one Messianic title, so well known--"Son of David" (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.30">Mt 20:30</reference>). Can there be a doubt that their faith fastened on such great Messianic promises as this, "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened," &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.5">Is 35:5</reference>)? and if so, this appeal to Him, as the Consolation of Israel, to do His predicted office, would fall with great weight upon the ears of Jesus. <div eID="gen25754" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e8a81c9fc0648820d0b9246f2e7311aaf893d6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13474"/><div sID="gen25755" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13474"/><hi type="bold">28. And when he was come into the house--</hi>To try their faith and patience, He seems to have made them no answer. But<div eID="gen25755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the blind men came to Him--</hi>which, no doubt, was what He desired.<div eID="gen25756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Jesus saith unto them, Believe ye that I am able to do this? they said unto him, Yea, Lord--</hi>Doubtless our Lord's design was not only to put their faith to the test by this question, but to deepen it, to raise their expectation of a cure, and so prepare them to receive it; and the cordial acknowledgment, so touchingly simple, which they immediately made to Him of His power to heal them, shows how entirely that object was gained. <div eID="gen25757" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa9b31f2bb3e5c171188de9ad9c25998d0931507: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13475"/><div sID="gen25758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13475"/><hi type="bold">29. Then touched he their eyes, saying, According to your faith be it unto you--</hi>not, Receive a cure proportioned to your faith, but, Receive this cure as granted to your faith. Thus would they carry about with them, in their restored vision, a gracious seal of the faith which drew it from their compassionate Lord. <div eID="gen25758" type="x-p"/>
entries.1506ac0fe9a38dd869ef223b27db993fde217041: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13476"/><div sID="gen25759" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13476"/><hi type="bold">30. And their eyes were opened: and Jesus straitly charged them--</hi>The expression is very strong, denoting great earnestness. <div eID="gen25759" type="x-p"/>
entries.19fb6d370a9d333e772b5dd393184af3118806a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13477"/><div sID="gen25760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13477"/><hi type="bold">31. But they, when they were departed, spread abroad his fame in all that country--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.8.4">Mt 8:4</reference>).<div eID="gen25760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25761" type="x-p"/> A Dumb Demoniac Healed (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.32-Matt.9.34">Mt 9:32-34</reference>). <div eID="gen25761" type="x-p"/>
entries.74181c9b8b979cd6f4ab60e1a42a23a6cb6f54ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13478"/><div sID="gen25762" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13478"/><hi type="bold">32. As they went out, behold, they brought to him a dumb man possessed with a devil--</hi>"demonized." The dumbness was not natural, but was the effect of the possession. <div eID="gen25762" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e1bb153440232f9038575288fecf5cf92e693fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13479"/><div sID="gen25763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13479"/><hi type="bold">33. And when the devil--</hi>demon.<div eID="gen25763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was cast out, the dumb spake--</hi>The particulars in this case are not given; the object being simply to record the instantaneous restoration of the natural faculties on the removal of the malignant oppression of them, the form which the popular astonishment took, and the very different effect of it upon another class.<div eID="gen25764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the multitudes marvelled, saying, It was never so seen in Israel--</hi>referring, probably, not to this case only, but to all those miraculous displays of healing power which seemed to promise a new era in the history of Israel. Probably they meant by this language to indicate, as far as they thought it safe to do so, their inclination to regard Him as the promised Messiah. <div eID="gen25765" type="x-p"/>
entries.73cc16cc6b6db824b7137b882878339174d98a68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13480"/><div sID="gen25766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13480"/><hi type="bold">34. But the Pharisees said, He casteth out devils through the prince of the devils--</hi>"the demons through the prince of the demons." This seems to be the first muttering of a theory of such miracles which soon became a fixed mode of calumniating them--a theory which would be ridiculous if it were not melancholy as an outburst of the darkest malignity. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.12.24">Mt 12:24</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen25766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Matt.9.35-Matt.10.5">Mt 9:35-10:5</reference>. Third Galilean Circuit--</hi>Mission of the Twelve Apostles.<div eID="gen25767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">As the Mission of the Twelve supposes the previous choice of them--</hi>of which our Evangelist gives no account, and which did not take place till a later stage of our Lord's public life--it is introduced here out of its proper place, which is after what is recorded in <reference osisRef="Luke.6.12-Luke.6.19">Lu 6:12-19</reference>.<div eID="gen25768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Third Galilean Circuit (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.35">Mt 9:35</reference>)--</hi>and probably the last. <div eID="gen25769" type="x-p"/>
entries.30486bfecb599ab23bc02940540f41a6563c2ecc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13481"/><div sID="gen25770" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13481"/><hi type="bold">35. And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease among the people--</hi>The italicized words are of more than doubtful authority here, and were probably introduced here from <reference osisRef="Matt.4.23">Mt 4:23</reference>. The language here is so identical with that used in describing the first circuit (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.23">Mt 4:23</reference>), that we may presume the work done on both occasions was much the same. It was just a further preparation of the soil, and a fresh sowing of the precious seed. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.4.23">Mt 4:23</reference>). To these fruitful journeyings of the Redeemer, "with healing in His wings," Peter no doubt alludes, when, in his address to the household of Cornelius, he spoke of "How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil: for God was with Him" (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.38">Ac 10:38</reference>).<div eID="gen25770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus Compassionating the Multitudes, Asks Prayer for Help (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.36-Matt.9.38">Mt 9:36-38</reference>). He had now returned from His preaching and healing circuit, and the result, as at the close of the first one, was the gathering of a vast and motley multitude around Him. After a whole night spent in prayer, He had called His more immediate disciples, and from them had solemnly chosen the twelve; then, coming down from the mountain, on which this was transacted, to the multitudes that waited for Him below, He had addressed to them--</hi>as we take it--that discourse which bears so strong a resemblance to the Sermon on the Mount that many critics take it to be the same. (See on <reference osisRef="Luke.6.12-Luke.6.49">Lu 6:12-49</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Matt.5.1">Mt 5:1</reference>, Introductory Remarks). Soon after this, it should seem, the multitudes still hanging on Him, Jesus is touched with their wretched and helpless condition, and acts as is now to be described. <div eID="gen25771" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b22f9a3a1ac531a4459319d03b16b650c444685: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13482"/><div sID="gen25772" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13482"/><hi type="bold">36. But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted--</hi>This reading, however, has hardly any authority at all. The true reading doubtless is, "were harassed."<div eID="gen25772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and were scattered abroad--</hi>rather, "lying about," "abandoned," or "neglected."<div eID="gen25773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as sheep, having no shepherd--</hi>their pitiable condition as wearied under bodily fatigue, a vast disorganized mass, being but a faint picture of their wretchedness as the victims of pharisaic guidance; their souls uncared for, yet drawn after and hanging upon Him. This moved the Redeemer's compassion. <div eID="gen25774" type="x-p"/>
entries.5769bfddebd178946574c149a99d7a79c40148bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13483"/><div sID="gen25775" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13483"/><hi type="bold">37. Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous--</hi>His eye doubtless rested immediately on the Jewish field, but this he saw widening into the vast field of "the world" (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.38">Mt 13:38</reference>), teeming with souls having to be gathered to Him.<div eID="gen25775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but the labourers--</hi>men divinely qualified and called to gather them in--"are few." <div eID="gen25776" type="x-p"/>
entries.172f3e15ba8b0d4589d184e6b508e765096c931d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13484"/><div sID="gen25777" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13484"/><hi type="bold">38. Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest--</hi>the great Lord and Proprietor of all. Compare <reference osisRef="John.15.1">Joh 15:1</reference>, "I am the true vine, and My Father is the husbandman."<div eID="gen25777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he will send forth labourers into his harvest--</hi>The word properly means "thrust forth"; but this emphatic sense disappears in some places, as in <reference osisRef="Matt.9.25">Mt 9:25</reference>, and <reference osisRef="John.10.4">Joh 10:4</reference>--"When He putteth forth His own sheep." (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.4.1">Mt 4:1</reference>). <chapter eID="Matt.9"/>

entries.1310acb6dbeda8b264478297dcf26656e1b642fb: <div eID="gen36877" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen36878" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36879" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36879" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36878" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36880" type="x-p"/> Christ heals a paralytic person at Capernaum, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.1-Mat.9.8">Mat 9:1-8</reference>. Calls Matthew, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.9-Mat.9.10">Mat 9:9-10</reference>. Eats with publicans and sinners, at which the Pharisees are offended, and he vindicates his conduct, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.11">Mat 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.12">Mat 9:12</reference>. The disciples of John come to him and inquire about fasting, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.14-Mat.9.17">Mat 9:14-17</reference>. A ruler requests him to heal his daughter, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.18">Mat 9:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.19">Mat 9:19</reference>. On his road to the ruler's house, he heals a diseased woman, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.20-Mat.9.22">Mat 9:20-22</reference>. Arriving at the ruler's house, he restores the young woman to life, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.23-Mat.9.26">Mat 9:23-26</reference>. Heals two blind men, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.27-Mat.9.31">Mat 9:27-31</reference>. Casts out a dumb demon, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.32-Mat.9.34">Mat 9:32-34</reference>. Preaches and works miracles in all the cities and villages, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.35">Mat 9:35</reference>. Is greatly affected at the desolate and dark state of the Jewish people, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.36">Mat 9:36</reference>. Exhorts his disciples to pray to God to send them proper instructers, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.37">Mat 9:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.38">Mat 9:38</reference>. <div eID="gen36880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36881" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen36881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36882" type="x-p"/> He came into his own city - Viz. Capernaum, where he seems to have had his common residence at the house of Peter. See <reference osisRef="Mat.4.13">Mat 4:13</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Mat.8.14">Mat 8:14</reference>. This verse properly belongs to the preceding chapter.
entries.e565ef0ef7478905587f35d6254b8be067b7a16c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen36882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36883" type="x-p"/> Sick of the palsy - See <reference osisRef="Mat.4.24">Mat 4:24</reference>. <div eID="gen36883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36884" type="x-p"/> Lying on a bed - Κλινης, a couch or sofa, such as they reclined on at meals. <div eID="gen36884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36885" type="x-p"/> Seeing their faith - The faith of the paralytic person, and the faith of those who brought him; see on <reference osisRef="Mar.2.4">Mar 2:4</reference> (note). <div eID="gen36885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36886" type="x-p"/> Be of good cheer - Θαρσει τεκνον, Son, take courage! Probably he began to despond, and Christ spoke thus to support his faith. <div eID="gen36886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36887" type="x-p"/> Thy sins be forgiven thee - Moral evil has been the cause of all the natural evil in the world. Christ goes to the source of the malady, which is sin; and to that as the procuring cause we should refer in all our afflictions. It is probable that this paralytic person had, in the earnest desires of his heart, entreated the cure of his soul, leaving his body to the care of others, as the first miracle of healing is wrought on his soul. In a state of helplessness, when we seek above all things to please God, by giving him our hearts, he often inspires others with the care of our temporal necessities. It may be necessary to be observed, that it was a maxim among the Jews that no diseased person could be healed till all his sins were blotted out. See Nedarim, fol. 41. Hence our Lord first forgives the sins, and then heals the body of the paralytic person. This appears to have been founded on <reference osisRef="Psa.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>. Who forgiveth all thine iniquities, and healeth all thy diseases. Here pardon precedes health. See also <reference osisRef="Psa.41.3">Psa 41:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.41.4">Psa 41:4</reference>. It may be observed, also, that most people are more in earnest about their souls when in sickness than in health, and therefore are more earnest in prayer for salvation.
entries.dcedb31caea5c5dd08558ab270bbaeef076416af: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen36887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36888" type="x-p"/> This man blasphemeth - Βλασφημεω comes either from βλαπτειν την φημην, to hurt or blast the reputation or credit of another, or from βαλλειν ταις φημαις, to smite with reports. Whenever it is used in reference to God, it simply signifies, to speak impiously of his nature, or attributes, or works. Injurious speaking is its proper translation when referred to man. <div eID="gen36888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36889" type="x-p"/> The scribes were the literati of that time; and their learning, because not used in dependence on God, rendered them proud, envious, and obstinate. Unsanctified knowledge has still the same effect: that light serves only to blind and lead men out of the way which is not joined with uprightness of heart. The most sacred truths often become an occasion of delusion, where men are under the government of their evil passions.
entries.9b991a1f51e090ef65518fc044da8fecbe323c72: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen36889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36890" type="x-p"/> Jesus knowing (ιδων seeing) their thoughts - In telling them what the thoughts of their hearts were, (for they had expressed nothing publicly), he gave them the fullest proof of his power to forgive sins; because God only can forgive sins, and God only can search and know the heart. Jesus pronounced the man's sins forgiven; and gave the scribes the fullest proof of his power to do so, by telling them what, in the secret of their souls, they thought on the subject. <div eID="gen36890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36891" type="x-p"/> God sounds the secrets of all hearts - no sin escapes his notice; how senseless then is the sinner to think he sins securely when unseen by men! Let us take heed to our hearts, as well as to our conduct, for God searches out and condemns all that does not spring from, and leads not to himself.
entries.ca4432a3c6ac1f0b157c0e1836e7dfb16af70091: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen36891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36892" type="x-p"/> For whether is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and walk? - Both are equally easy, and equally difficult; for both require unlimited power to produce them. And every thing is equally easy to that power which is unlimited. A universe can be as easily produced by a single act of the Divine will as the smallest elementary part of matter. <div eID="gen36892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36893" type="x-p"/> The common punctuation of the above passage almost destroys the sense: the comma should be placed after easier, and to say, made the first part of the question.
entries.c2956b37734092cedbd767336660e0f1bed62520: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen36893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36894" type="x-p"/> But that ye may know, etc. - External miracles are the proofs of internal ones. Three miracles are wrought in this case. (I mean, by miracle, something produced or known that no power is capable of but that which is omnipotent, and no knowledge adequate to but that which is omniscient). The miracles are these: 1st. The remission of the poor man's sins. 2d. The discernment of the secret thoughts of the scribes. 3d. The restoring of the paralytic, in an instant, to perfect soundness. <div eID="gen36894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36895" type="x-p"/> Thus one miracle becomes the proof and establishment of another. Never was a clearer proof of omnipotent energy and mercy brought under the senses of man. Here is an absolutely perfect miracle wrought; and here are absolute incontestable proofs that the miracle was wrought; and the conclusion is the fullest demonstration of the Divinity of the ever-blessed Jesus. <div eID="gen36895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36896" type="x-p"/> Arise, take up thy bed - Being enabled to obey this command was the public proof that the man was made whole. Such a circumstance should not pass without improvement. A man gives proof of his conversion from sin to God who imitates this paralytic person. He who does not rise and stand upright, but either continues grovelling on the earth, or falls back as soon as he is got up, is not yet cured of his spiritual palsy. When we see a penitent enabled to rejoice in hope of God's glory, and to walk in the way of his commandments, he affords us all the proof which we can reasonably require, that his conversion is real: the proof sufficient to satisfy himself is the witness of the Holy Spirit in his own heart; but this is a matter of which those who are without cannot judge: they must form their opinion from his conduct, and judge of the tree by its fruits.
entries.9354157e0aed733fa2bbb6efb8414cdd76a314e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen36896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36897" type="x-p"/> When the multitudes saw it, they marveled - Instead of εθαυμασαν, wondered, the Codex Vatic. and Cod. Bezae, with several other MSS. and versions, have εφοβηθησαν, feared. In the Gothic, and one copy of the Itala, both readings are conjoined, thus: And the multitudes seeing it, wondered and feared, and glorified God. Wondered at the miracle; feared to offend against such power and goodness; and glorified God for the works of mercy which he had wrought. <div eID="gen36897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36898" type="x-p"/> That which to the doctors of the law, the worldly-wise and prudent, is a matter of scandal, is to the humble an occasion of glorifying the Most High. Divine things make a deeper impression on the hearts of the simple multitude than on those of the doctors, who, puffed up with a sense of their own wisdom, refuse to receive the truth as it is in Jesus. The conversion of one rebellious soul is a greater miracle, and more to be admired than all that can be wrought on inanimate creatures. He who sees a sinner converted from the error of his way sees a miracle wrought by eternal power and goodness. May such miracles be multiplied!
entries.3d92a0f14e86121183860372a4effa608cee309c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen36898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36899" type="x-p"/> Named Matthew - Generally supposed to be the same who wrote this history of our blessed Lord. Mathai signifies a gift in Syriac; probably so named by his parents as implying a gift from God. <div eID="gen36899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36900" type="x-p"/> The receipt of custom - The custom-house, τελωνιον - the place where the taxes levied by the Romans of the Jews, were collected. <div eID="gen36900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36901" type="x-p"/> Follow me - That is, become my disciple. <div eID="gen36901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36902" type="x-p"/> And he arose, and followed him - How blessed it is to be obedient to the first call of Christ - how much happiness and glory are lost by delays, though conversion at last may have taken place!
entries.53071d3720482917a44ce3bcae95715b4824971d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen36902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36903" type="x-p"/> Sat at meat in the house - Viz. of Matthew, who it appears, from <reference osisRef="Luk.5.29">Luk 5:29</reference>, made a great feast on the occasion, thus testifying his gratitude for the honor done him; and that his friends and acquaintances might profit by the teaching of his new master, he invites them to the entertainment that was honored by the presence of Christ. His companions, it appears, were not of the most creditable kind. They were tax-gatherers (see <reference osisRef="Mat.5.46">Mat 5:46</reference>) and sinners, αμαρτωλοι, a word which I believe in general signifies heathens, throughout the Gospels, and in several other parts of the New Testament. See, among others, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.19">Mat 11:19</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mat.26.45">Mat 26:45</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mar.2.15-Mar.2.17">Mar 2:15-17</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mar.14.41">Mar 14:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.5.30-Luk.5.32">Luk 5:30-32</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Luk.6.32-Luk.6.34">Luk 6:32-34</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Luk.7.34">Luk 7:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.7.37">Luk 7:37</reference>, (note); <reference osisRef="Luk.7.39">Luk 7:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.15.1">Luk 15:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.15.2">Luk 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.15.7">Luk 15:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.15.10">Luk 15:10</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Luk.19.7">Luk 19:7</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Luk.24.7">Luk 24:7</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Joh.9.16">Joh 9:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.9.24">Joh 9:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.9.25">Joh 9:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.9.31">Joh 9:31</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Rom.5.8">Rom 5:8</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Gal.2.15">Gal 2:15</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Heb.7.26">Heb 7:26</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.18">1Pet 4:18</reference> (note); in most, if not all of which places, it evidently refers to the character or state of a Gentile, or Heathen. See also the notes on these passages.
entries.55e456fa4957391ed34717c4472cedddcf79b73f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen36903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36904" type="x-p"/> When the Pharisees saw it - He who, like a Pharisee, never felt himself indebted to infinite mercy for his own salvation, is rarely solicitous about the salvation of others. The grace of Christ alone inspires the soul with true benevolence. The self-righteous Pharisees considered it equal to legal defilement to sit in company with tax-gatherers and heathens. It is certain that those who fear God should not associate, through choice, with the workers of iniquity, and should only be found with them when transacting their secular business requires it, or when they have the prospect of doing good to their souls.
entries.199c5dc41a27b59435ed6faf40952236eddf264e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen36904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36905" type="x-p"/> They that be whole need not a physician - A common proverb, which none could either misunderstand or misapply. Of it the reader may make the following use: - <div eID="gen36905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36906" type="x-p"/> 1. Jesus Christ represents himself here as the sovereign Physician of souls. <div eID="gen36906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36907" type="x-p"/> 2. That all stand in need of his healing power. <div eID="gen36907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36908" type="x-p"/> 3. That men must acknowledge their spiritual maladies, and the need they have of his mercy, in order to be healed by him. <div eID="gen36908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36909" type="x-p"/> 4. That it is the most inveterate and dangerous disease the soul can be afflicted with to imagine itself whole, when the sting of death, which is sin, has pierced it through in every part, infusing its poison every where.
entries.90e274d3d2547d06c22dc37eece1a69a9895876e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen36909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36910" type="x-p"/> I will have mercy, and not sacrifice - Quoted from <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sam 15:22</reference>. These are remarkable words. We may understand them as implying, 1st. That God prefers an act of mercy, shown to the necessitous, to any act of religious worship to which the person might be called at that time. Both are good; but the former is the greater good, and should be done in preference to the other. 2dly. That the whole sacrificial system was intended only to point out the infinite mercy of God to fallen man, in his redemption by the blood of the new covenant. And 3dly. That we should not rest in the sacrifices, but look for the mercy and salvation prefigured by them. This saying was nervously translated by our ancestors, I will mild-heartedness, and not sacrifice. <div eID="gen36910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36911" type="x-p"/> Go ye and learn - צא ולמד tse velimmed, a form of speech in frequent use among the rabbins, when they referred to any fact or example in the Sacred Writings. Nothing tends more to humble pretenders to devotion than to show them that they understand neither Scripture nor religion, when, relying on external performances, they neglect love to God and man, which is the very soul and substance of true religion. True holiness has ever consisted in faith working by love. <div eID="gen36911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36912" type="x-p"/> I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners - Most of the common editions add, εις μετανοιαν, unto repentance; but this is omitted in the Codex Vatic. and Bezae, sixteen others, both the Syriac, both the Persic, Ethiop. Armen. Gothic, Anglo-Saxon, all the Itala except three, the Vulgate, Clemens Roman, Origen, Basil, Jerome, Augustin, Ambrose, and Barnabas. The omission is approved by Mill and Bengel. Griesbach leaves it out of the text.
entries.d0faaa9481efe79e6d307d8f2006014103353814: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen36912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36913" type="x-p"/> Thy disciples fast not? - Probably meaning that they did not fast so frequently as the others did, or for the same purposes, which is very likely, for the Pharisees had many superstitious fasts. They fasted in order to have lucky dreams, to obtain the interpretation of a dream, or to avert the evil import of a dream. They also fasted often, in order to obtain the things they wished for. The tract, Taanith is full of these fasts, and of the wonders performed thus by the Jewish doctors.
entries.93f3f1c8d5d2aeb4640e93c19c23d01ad10c0b46: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen36913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36914" type="x-p"/> Can the children of the bride-chamber - Νυμφωνος. Or, νυμφιου, bridegroom, as the Cod. Bezae and several versions have it. These persons were the companions of the bridegroom, who accompanied him to the house of his father-in-law when he went to bring the bride to his own home. The marriage-feast among the Jews lasted seven days; but the new married woman was considered to be a bride for thirty days. Marriage feasts were times of extraordinary festivity, and even of riot, among several people of the east. <div eID="gen36914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36915" type="x-p"/> When the bridegroom shall be taken from them, etc. - There was one annual fast observed in the primitive Church, called by our ancestors the spring fast, and, by us, Lent; by the Greeks τεσσερακοϚη, and by the Latins, Quadrigessima. This fast is pretended to be kept by many, in the present day, in commemoration of our Lord's forty days' fast in the wilderness; but it does not appear that, in the purest ages of the primitive Church, genuine Christians ever pretended that their quadrigessimal fast was kept for the above purpose. Their fast was kept merely to commemorate the time during which Jesus Christ lay under the power of death, which was about Forty Hours; and it was in this sense they understood the words of this text: the days will come, etc. With them, the bridegroom meant Christ: the time in which he was taken away, his crucifixion, death, and the time he lay in the grave. Suppose him dying about twelve o'clock on what is called Friday, and that he rose about four on the morning of his own day, (St. John says, Early, while it was yet dark, <reference osisRef="Mat.20.1">Mat 20:1</reference>), the interim makes forty hours, which was the true primitive Lent, or quadrigessimal fast. It is true that many in the primitive Church were not agreed on this subject, as Socrates, in his Church History, book v. chap. 22, says, "Some thought they should fast one day; others two; others more." Different Churches also were divided concerning the length of the time, some keeping it three, others five, and others seven weeks; and the historian himself is puzzled to know why they all agreed in calling these fasts, differing so much in their duration, by the name of Quadrigessima, or forty days' fast: the plain obvious reason appears to me to have been simply this: They put Days in the place of Hours; and this absurdity continues in some Christian Churches to the present day. For more on fasting, see <reference osisRef="Mat.6.16">Mat 6:16</reference>.
entries.6ce9c4aa10f924b3562cd3eb207521cf11cf58d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen36915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36916" type="x-p"/> No man putteth a piece of new cloth - Ουδεις δε επιβαλλει επιβλημα ρακους αγναφου επι ιματιω παλαιω. No man putteth a patch of unscoured cloth upon an old garment. This is the most literal translation I can give of this verse, to convey its meaning to those who cannot consult the original. Ρακος αγναφον is that cloth which has not been scoured, or which has not passed under the hand of the fuller, who is called γναφευς in Greek: and επιβλημα signifies a piece put on, or what we commonly term a patch. <div eID="gen36916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36917" type="x-p"/> It - taketh from the garment - Instead of closing up the rent, it makes a larger, by tearing away with it the whole breadth of the cloth over which it was laid; αιρει γαρ το πληρωμα αυτου - it taketh its fullness or whole breadth from the garment; this I am persuaded is the meaning of the original, well expressed by the Latin, or Itala of the C. Bezae, Tollit enim plenitudo ejus de vestimento. "It takes away its fullness from the garment."
entries.cad07edf7fa0610f83a32fc4d8bf27f4d42362dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen36917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36918" type="x-p"/> New wine into old bottles - It is still the custom, in the eastern countries, to make their bottles of goat skins: if these happened to be old, and new wine were put into them, the violence of the fermentation must necessarily burst them; and therefore newly made bottles were employed for the purpose of putting that wine in which had not yet gone through its state of fermentation. The institutes of Christ, and those of the Pharisees, could never be brought to accord: an attempt to combine the two systems would be as absurd as it would be destructive. The old covenant made way for the new, which was its completion and its end; but with that old covenant the new cannot be incorporated. <div eID="gen36918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36919" type="x-p"/> Christian prudence requires that the weak, and newly converted, should be managed with care and tenderness. To impose such duties and mortifications as are not absolutely necessary to salvation, before God has properly prepared the heart by his grace for them, is a conduct as absurd and ruinous as putting a piece of raw, unscoured cloth on an old garment; it is, in a word, requiring the person to do the work of a man, while as yet he is but a little child. Preachers of the Gospel, and especially those who are instruments in God's hand of many conversions, have need of much heavenly wisdom, that they may know to watch over, guide, and advise those who are brought to a sense of their sin and danger. How many auspicious beginnings have been ruined by men's proceeding too hastily, endeavoring to make their own designs take place, and to have the honor of that success themselves which is due only to God.
entries.cb0bb357fc20e2f22ebab870d3d0145fa38931ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen36919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36920" type="x-p"/> A certain ruler - There were two officers in the synagogue, חזן הכנסת chazan ha-ceneseth, the bishop or overseer of the congregation; and ראש הכנסת rosh ha-ceneseth, the head or ruler of the congregation. The chazan takes the book of the Law, and gives it to the rosh, or ruler; and he appoints who shall read the different sections, etc. Jairus, who is the person intended here, was, in this latter sense, the ruler or governor of one of the synagogues, probably at Capernaum. See <reference osisRef="Mar.5.22">Mar 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.8.41">Luk 8:41</reference>. <div eID="gen36920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36921" type="x-p"/> My daughter is even now dead - Or, my daughter was just now dying; αρτι ετελευτησεν, or, is by this time dead: i.e. as Mr. Wakefield properly observes, She was so ill when I left home that she must be dead by this time. This turn of the expression reconciles the account given here with that in Mark and Luke. Michaelis conjectures that, in the Hebrew original, the words must have stood thus, עתה מתה atah matah, which, without the points, may signify either, She is dead, or She is dying. <div eID="gen36921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36922" type="x-p"/> To be successful in our applications to God by prayer, four things are requisite; and this ruler teaches us what they are. <div eID="gen36922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36923" type="x-p"/> First, A man should place himself in the presence of God - he came unto him. <div eID="gen36923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36924" type="x-p"/> Secondly, He should humble himself sincerely before God - he fell down before him - at his feet. <reference osisRef="Mar.5.22">Mar 5:22</reference>. <div eID="gen36924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36925" type="x-p"/> Thirdly, He should lay open his wants with a holy earnestness - he besought him greatly. <reference osisRef="Mar.5.23">Mar 5:23</reference>. <div eID="gen36925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36926" type="x-p"/> Fourthly, he should have unbounded confidence in the power and goodness of Christ that his request shall be granted - put thy hand upon her, and she shall live. <div eID="gen36926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36927" type="x-p"/> He who comes in this way to God, for salvation, is sure to be heard. Imposition of hands was a rite anciently used by the servants of God, through which heavenly influences were conveyed to the bodies and souls of men. This rite is still used in certain Churches; but, as there is no Holy Ghost communicated by it, some suppose it may be as well omitted. But why is this? Is it not because there is an unfaithfulness in the person who lays on hands, or an unfitness in him on whom they are laid?
